ii

Staff training and development has remained as one of the key objectives of my Office. This
was made possible with the assistance of the African Organisation of English-speaking
Supreme Audit Institutions (AFROSAI-E) to which Zimbabwe is a member, Swedish National
Audit Office (SNAO) for technical support and other Development Partners, study visits to other
Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs), Professional Accountants Bodies and other stakeholders. A
number of training programmes, technical updates and Continuous Professional
Developments (CPDs) were attended by my staff in order to keep them up to date with the
developments taking place in the auditing profession.
Audit guidance materials were
developed and updated during the year in order to enhance the quality of audits.
4.
BASIS OF PREPARATION OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

Management of public funds is governed primarily by the Constitution of Zimbabwe and the
Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19]. Central Government uses cash accounting
basis for Appropriation Accounts and accruals accounting for Fund Accounts.

5.
TRANSITIONAL ARRANGEMENTS - MIGRATION TO IPSAS FINANCIAL REPORTING
FRAMEWORK

The Government has adopted the accrual based International Public Sector Accounting
Standards (IPSAS) as its reporting framework for Central Government which should be fully
implemented by January 2025 according to the implementation road map. According to
Treasury Circular number 4 of 2022, the MDAs were to migrate to the IPSAS financial reporting
framework with effect from January 1, 2024 and produce annual IPSAS transitional financial
statements for the year ended December 31, 2024 for review by April 30, 2025. My office is
currently reviewing the transitional financial statements.

6.
AUDIT APPROACH

I conducted my statutory audits in accordance with the International Standards of Supreme
Audit Institutions (ISSAIs) and the International Standards on Auditing (ISAs). These
Standards require that I comply with ethical requirements, plan and perform the audit to obtain
reasonable assurance whether the financial statements are free from material misstatement.
My audit approach was designed to enable me to express an opinion on the financial
statements.
All aspects of the entities’ activities and procedures may not have been examined. I consider
maintenance of adequate internal controls to be the responsibility of management. My work
cannot therefore, be expected to identify all weaknesses in the systems and procedures, which
a special investigation directed at those areas might reveal. As to the possibility of fraud, I plan
my audits to have a reasonable expectation of its disclosure if the potential effects of the fraud
would be material in the financial statements. However, there are many kinds of fraudulent
activities, particularly those involving defalcation, forgery, collusion and management override
of controls, which would be unreasonable to expect the normal audit to uncover.
I carried out audits at 39 Head Offices of Ministries and Commissions. I also visited outstations
of some of the Ministries and government departments that are decentralized. Results of the
audit of Provincial and District stations are included in my findings in this report.
iii

In 2024, the total number of stations were 4 715 and I visited 169 Provincial and District offices
as compared to 196 visited in 2023. Financial constraints adversely affected the number of
stations visited. Resources permitting, in 2025, I would like to increase audit visits to
outstations, given that, a lot of functions have been decentralised. Refer to the pie chart below
and Annexure A for details.



7.
CERTIFICATION OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

I certify that I have examined the Appropriation Accounts, Finance and Revenue Statements,
other supporting returns and Fund Accounts of Zimbabwe in accordance with the Constitution
of Zimbabwe Amendment (No 20) Act 2013, the Audit Office Act [Chapter 22:18] and the Public
Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19] and other relevant Statutory Instruments.
AUDIT OPINION

I conducted my statutory audits in accordance with the International Standards of Supreme
Audit Institutions (ISSAIs). The principal objective of my audit procedures is to enable me to
express an opinion on the truth and fairness of the financial statements submitted by Ministries,
Commissions and Funds. An audit opinion is based on the concept of reasonable assurance.
It is not a guarantee that the financial statements are free of misstatements. Where I have
issued an unmodified / clean, qualified and adverse opinion, I believe that the audit evidence I
have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide the basis for my opinion of the respective
financial statements. Where an entity received a disclaimer of opinion its merely because l was
unable to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence to express an opinion.
A total of 131 (80:2023) financial statements are included in this report. The audit opinions
on the financial statements are shown on the table and pie chart below:

Clean/Unmodified- The financial statements contain no material misstatements.

Qualified- The financial statements contain material misstatements in specific amounts, or
there is insufficient evidence to conclude that specific amounts included in the financial
statements are not materially misstated.
Adverse- The financial statements contain material misstatements that are not confined to
specific amounts, or the misstatements represent a substantial portion of the financial
statements.
Disclaimer- The auditor has not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to
provide a basis of an audit opinion. The lack of sufficient evidence is not confined to specific
amounts, or represents a substantial portion of the information contained in the financial
statements.

consolidated into one report by the Accountant-General in terms of Section 35 (12) of the Public
Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19].

Ministries and Commissions are required to submit their financial statements by January 31,
and supporting statements by February 28 of each year. However, some of the financial
statements were not submitted for audit on time, hence they are not included in my report. At
the time of concluding this report in June 2025, audits of other twenty-three (23) financial
statements were in progress, audits of thirty-one (31) financial statements had not commenced
due to manpower shortage and late submission of financial statements, while thirty-eight (38)
financial statements had not been submitted for audit. Two (2) financial statements were
withdrawn at signing stage.

I also carried and concluded five (5) Value for Money Audits and the reports are tabled
separately.

In addition, my Office audited 10 financial statements of Donor Funded Projects that are
implemented under some MDAs whose findings are not in this report.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS

I wish to acknowledge efforts rendered by all the Accounting Officers, Chief Executive Officers,
Receivers of Revenue, Development partners, Printflow (Pvt) Ltd and other stakeholders that
made it possible for me to submit my Report.

Finally, I extend my sincere appreciation to the Audit Office Board for their support,
management and staff for their continued commitment and dedication to duty.

                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This report outlines results of my audit of financial statements which comprise Appropriation
Accounts, Finance and Revenue Statements, Statements of Comprehensive Income and
Statements of Financial Position and Statements of Cash Flows. A combined financial and
compliance audit was conducted with the aim of improving public sector transparency,
accountability, compliance with regulations, good corporate governance and service delivery.
I also audited the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) which is an Enterprise
Resource Planning platform used by Ministries and Commissions for processing of financial
transactions. I reviewed the controls of the Information Technology system to gain assurance
about their adequacy and effectiveness.
The financial audit seeks to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial
statements as a whole are free from material misstatements, whether due to fraud or error, and
to issue an auditor’s report that includes my opinion.
I also considered compliance with legislative provisions which directly and materially affect the
financial statements and whether the provisions in the applicable laws, rules, regulations and
instructions issued by a competent authority were complied with.
My report highlights, the key audit findings, risks and recommendations. These findings were
communicated to and discussed with management and those charged with governance. The
findings were classified under the following headings: governance issues, revenue collection
and debt recovery, compensation of employees, procurement of goods and services,
management of assets.
My audit also included an evaluation of the budget utilisation and funding received by the
various MDAs to assess extent to which mandates were fulfilled.
I evaluated the actions taken and determined the extent to which prior year audit findings had
been addressed. Those charged with governance in the various institutions are urged to pay
attention to matters raised herein, so as to improve public sector transparency, accountability,
good corporate governance and service delivery. It is expected that the impact of addressing
my findings will have a positive effect on the lives of the citizens.
I appreciate efforts made by Government in the form of statutory/structural reforms, which
included development and implementation of National Development Strategy (NDS) 1 towards
the attainment of Vision 2030, the requirements by the Office of the President and Cabinet for
senior management to sign performance contracts. In addition, the signing of integrity pledges
and the establishment of integrity committees will go a long way in improving accountability
and promoting sound corporate governance.

1.
Conversion of Financial Transactions from ZWL to ZWG


The Government of Zimbabwe changed currency from ZWL to Zimbabwe Gold (ZWG) effective April
6, 2024. The reporting currency for the 2024 financial statements was the ZWG. Ministries,
Departments and Agencies (MDAs) were supposed to produce financial statements for the whole
financial year in one currency (ZWG). This meant translating the ZWL transactions to ZWG. To
achieve this, Treasury provided guidance to MDAs on how the ZWL financial transactions were to be
translated. However, the circular was not uniformly applied by MDAs. Nearly all MDAs withdrew and
resubmitted financial statements during audit, some withdrew and resubmitted more than four (4)
times. Refer to Annexure C for details.

2.
Budget Utilisation and Budgetary Control

The initial 2024 Voted funds as per the Appropriation (2024) Act, 2023 for the thirty-two (32)
Appropriation Accounts included in this report was ZWG41 122 109 960. Unallocated Reserve
Transfers amounting to ZWG14 547 940 934 were subsequently made to almost all MDAs. An
analysis of the Appropriation Accounts indicated that some MDAs that received additional budget
allocations had not exhausted their original budgets signaling ineffective management of budget.
Total expenditure for mentioned votes amounted to ZW43 874 983 672 leaving a net
underspending of ZWG11 794 703 221.

In addition, the budget allocation for Constitutional and Statutory Appropriations was
ZWG11 187 409 335 with additional budget allocation of ZWG4 763 839 455. Total expenditure
amounted to ZWG11 113 702 575 resulting in an underspending of ZWG1 282 810 505.

The 32 MDAs were given a total budget of ZWG55 669 686 893 and utilized ZWG43 878 983 672,

3.
Accounting System

There was a down time of the Public Financial Management Systems (PFMS) during the country
changeover of currency from ZWL$ to Zimbabwe Gold (ZWG) for almost five (5) months (April to
August 2024). During that time most MDAs operated outside the PFMS. The financial information
that would have been processed outside the system was not uploaded onto the system in some
cases. Such information would misstate expenditure figures.

4.        Open Items

Review of the Public Financial Management System indicated that most MDAs had open items. Open
items or uncleared entries disrupt budgetary control as they represent unconfirmed or unresolved
expenditures. This would make it difficult to track actual expenditure against allocated funds. Treasury
Circular No. 1 of 2025 requires Accounting Officers to clear all open items in the system before
preparation of bank reconciliations, annual returns and financial statements to ensure completeness
and alignment of financial information. Most MDAs had challenges in clearing such transactions and
were seeking Treasury assistance in clearing the open items.

There is need for Ministry of Finance to relook into the issue of releasing budget without the
necessary cash resource as MDAs spend a lot of time and financial resources going through
procurement processes and some receiving goods that would not be funded. This would require
reversing all the unfunded transactions at the end of the year.

5.
Direct Payments

Direct payments amounting to US$1 986 391 797 were made to service providers on behalf of the
MDAs by Treasury during the 2024 financial year. However, MDAs accounted for US$1 388 673 713,
leaving a balance of US$597 718 082 as at June 18, 2025. In some instances, the payments were
not uploaded onto the PFMS. MDAs expenditure was understated by the direct payments. Refer to
Annexure E.
6 Payment Arrears
Thirty -nine (39) Ministries, Departments and Agencies had arrear payments amounting to
ZWG14 742 728 388, US$61 046 894, ZAR733 058 and €214 709. Some of these amounts have
been outstanding since 2021. These arrear payments have been on the increase. The accumulation
of arrears if left unattended, erodes the budget of the subsequent year and negatively impacts on
Government service delivery and reputation. There is need to prioritise funding of MDAs to avoid
accumulation of arrears. Refer to Annexure F.
ix


7
Fuel Management

Cases of loss of fuel were on the increase. These were attributed to control weaknesses in fuel
management ranging from non-maintenance of fuel registers, inconsistent fuel recordings, non-
performance of fuel reconciliations, absence of segregation of duties and weak supervisory checks.
In this report, seven (7) MDAs had issues on fuel management. Measures around fuel management
should be enhanced.

8.
Sub-Paymaster General’s Account Reconciliations (Government Paying Accounts)

Differences were noted on expenditure reported between the Sub-Paymaster General’s Accounts
of certain MDAs and their corresponding Appropriation Accounts. These differences had not been
resolved by June 5, 2025. MDAs are encouraged to reconcile the Sub-PMG’s Account with the
Appropriation Account, as this would improve the accuracy of the financial information.

 9       Undelivered Motor Vehicles and Other Assets

Non-delivery of procured goods is still a cause for concern in Government. Some MDAs had
undelivered goods dating back to 2021. I noted that contract monitoring was not effectively done
as provisions of the contract on non-performance by the supplier were not invoked.

A total of forty (40) vehicles, seventeen (17) fire trucks, eighty-three (83) desktops, seventy-five
(75) laptops and various office furniture paid for between 2021 and 2024 had not been delivered
as at May 30, 2025. There is risk of excessive contract price variations if payments and
deliveries are not made within the agreed contract period. Service delivery was also
compromised as the assets are tools of trade required for the well-functioning of MDAs. Refer to
Annexure G

10       Management of Assets and Government Properties

The issue of maintenance of Assets registers remains a challenge in Ministries and their respective
Fund Accounts. In some instances, Assets registers were not in place, had incorrect quantities
recorded, did not have serial numbers, date of purchase and location to facilitate identification of
the assets. Ministries are urged to maintain and update Assets registers to guard against loss of
state property and ensure smooth transition to IPSAS financial reporting framework.
12
Revenue Collection and Debt Recovery

Revenue collection remained low in 2024. The outstanding revenue from seven (7) ministries
amounted to ZWG20 221 636 and US$14 560 697. Adequate steps and strategies were not being
taken to collect outstanding revenue and recover outstanding debts. MDAs should continuously
engage debtors for the recovery of outstanding revenue. Government should also monitor and
disclose investments made in various companies and any dividends paid should be deposited in
the Sub-Exchequer Account.

Finding

Treasury, any deficiencies or irregularities.

1.2    Grain Distribution

Findings
An examination of grain distribution records in Masvingo Province, Manicaland Province,
Matabeleland North Province, and Matabeleland South Province revealed that grain
withdrawal slips at the District Offices and Grain Marketing Board tax invoices had
discrepancies of 14 428 bags of maize which translates to 721 tonnes. The quantity authorised
for issue by the District Offices differed from the quantity of maize issued by the GMB Depots.
This could have been due to lack of proper measuring mechanism as GMB resorted to
averaging the weight of few bags of the total stock of grain using a digital scale and took it to
be representative of the whole stock.
Additionally, most GMB depots had no weigh bridges and some were not functional.
Risk/Implication
Grain might be abused as there is no exact way of measuring the quantities of maize
dispatched.
Recommendation
Management should implement a proper way of measuring quantities of grain before being
dispatched.
 Management Response

The observation is acknowledged. This problem is prevalent across all the GMB depots
and arises from the failure by GMB to re-bag grain which has been received from
farmers. Management will ensure that re-bagging is done to avoid these discrepancies
and each district will be called upon to reconcile its grain withdrawal slips to the
dispatch notes to ensure that the Ministry is charged for the actual grain withdrawn.

1.3    Underutilisation of Resources

Finding
The National Drought Fund did not utilise all the Funds that were disbursed by Treasury during
the year under review. ZWL$23 974 073 was recalled by Treasury due to non- utilisation. The
amount could have gone a long way in availing the much-needed resources to mitigate the
impact of the food deficit in the country. Section 36 (1) of the Public Finance Management
(Treasury Instructions), 2019 requires Accounting Officers to monitor the performance of the
budget regularly to ensure the delivery of expected results and to address any deviations from
their line ministry’s targets.

Risk/Implication
The Fund could fail to achieve its mandate and carry out the programs and activities that were
planned during the period under review.

The Ministry should regularly monitor the budget to ensure delivery of planned activities and
avoid failure to utilise the resources availed by Treasury.

tender process did not move fast enough, resulting in an unexpected balance.

PUBLIC FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM 2023-2024

Background Information

The Public Financial Management System (PFMS) is an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)
system that processes financial transactions and produces reports for all the Ministries. It was
implemented in 1999.
The Ministry of Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion is responsible for
the system and the Accountant-General is the one in charge of the PFMS. The infrastructure
of the system is managed by the Ministry of Information, Communication Technology, Postal
and Courier Services. The following modules were implemented:
a)Financial Accounting (FI)-for external financial reporting.
b)Materials Management (MM)-for procurement.
c) Sales and Distribution (SD)-for receipting.
d)Customer Relationship Management (CRM)-for managing online services.
e)Grants Management Module-for managing grants from cooperating partners.
f)Business Planning and Consolidation (BPC)-for financial planning.
g)Business Intelligence (BI)- for decision-making.

OBJECTIVE OF THE PUBLIC FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM

The objective of the PFMS is to process financial transactions and produce reports for all the
Ministries and Government Departments.

I conducted an audit to determine the effectiveness of general information technology
controls for the PFMS. The audit also aimed at ascertaining the implementation and
operating effectiveness of application controls in terms of Information Systems Audit and
Control Association (ISACA) Standards.

I have audited the General and Application Controls of the Public Financial Management
System for the period ended December 31, 2024.

Below are issues noted during the audit:
1     GOVERNANCE ISSUES
1.1
Information System Steering Committee
Findings

For the fourth year running, there was no evidence of the existence of an Information
Technology (IT) Steering Committee at the Ministry of Finance, Economic Development and
Investment Promotion as the terms of reference for the Committee were not availed for my
inspection nor was there evidence of the appointment of approved membership of the
Committee. Further, minutes of the Committee meetings were not availed for audit.
Responding to the same issue in my previous audit report, management indicated that the
Committee would resume sitting on March 3, 2023. However, as at January 15, 2025, there
was no evidence that the Committee had convened any meetings.

This was contrary to best practice which advocates that top management demonstrates
leadership and commitment by establishing an IT Steering Committee comprising senior
managers to facilitate alignment of entity strategic goals and information technology goals and
also assist in providing oversight over Information Systems activities.
85


Risks/Implications
IT related concerns may not be timeously attended to and resolved.
Project overruns on IT related projects could occur due to lack of oversight.
Recommendation

The Ministry should establish a formal IT Steering Committee that meets on a regular basis to
consider IT related concerns and review projects in progress.
Management Response
The approval was obtained to resuscitate the Steering Committee of the Public
Financial Management System.
1.2
Capacitation of the Internal Audit Function
Finding
The Internal Audit Function of the Ministry of Finance, Economic Development and Investment
Promotion did not carry out Information Systems audits of the Public Finance Management
System (PFMS) because it was not capacitated to perform the audits. Provisions of the Public
Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19] requires the Internal Auditor to monitor the financial
administration procedures of the Ministry to ensure adequate internal checks and controls are
observed.
Risk/Implication
Information System control deficiencies could go undetected if regular audits of the PFMS
system are not carried out.
Recommendation
The Internal Audit Function should be capacitated to carry out Information System Audits of
the PFMS system.
Management Response
The Ministry of Finance had no capacity at the time of audit, and now they have been
capacitated and ready to audit the PFMS.
1.3
PFMS Organogram
Finding
At the time of the audit, there was no organogram for the PFMS Unit which was availed for
audit inspection. Security best practice states that information security is achieved by
implementing a suitable set of controls, including policies, processes, procedures,
organisational structures, software and hardware functions.

Risk/Implication

There could be lack of separation of duties, ambiguity in business rules and inconsistency in
86

processes and procedures.
Recommendation
There is a need to develop an organogram to implement adequate information security
controls.
Management Response
The finding is noted. The organogram has been created and it will be implemented in
consultation with the Human Resources Department and/or the Public Service
Commission.
Evaluation of Management Response
The organogram submitted for audit inspection did not represent the structure existing in the
PFMS Unit.
2      COMPUTER OPERATIONS AND DISASTER RECOVERY PLANNING
2.1
Data Centre Operating Policy Manual
Finding
The data centre was operating without an approved data centre operating policy and manual.
I raised the same matter in my previous report but it remained outstanding at the time of
concluding my audit in January 2025. It is standard IT good practice to have an operating
manual that has detailed instructions on how to perform various tasks related to the data centre
operations such as equipment startup and shutdown procedures, maintenance routines,
troubleshooting guides and disaster recovery protocols.
Risk/Implication
Lack of clear Operating Policy and Procedures Manual may result in inconsistent practices and
sub-standard operation.
Recommendation
A Data Centre Operating Policy and a Manual should be developed and approved in line with
IT good practice to ensure operational efficiency and consistency.
Management Response
A draft Data Centre Operating Policy and a Manual have been developed and awaiting
approval.
2.2
Training of Data Centre Operators on Security Violations
Findings
Personnel manning the Data Centre were not trained on how to respond to different types of
fire emergencies or security violations.
Furthermore, there were no emergency response teams appointed and equipped with basic
tools to enable them to co-ordinate emergency evacuation activities. Fire Drills were last done
in 2021.
87

This was against best practice which requires all employees of the organisation and, where
relevant, contractors to receive appropriate awareness education and training and regular
updates in organisational policies and procedures, as relevant for their job function.
Risks/Implications
There may be inadequate response in the event of fire outbreak and other emergencies.
Equipment and personnel may be lost if there are no fire marshals or emergency response
teams in place.
Recommendations
Personnel manning the Data Centre should be trained on how to respond in case of fire
outbreak or other emergencies.
Fire Marshals or emergency response teams should be appointed, equipped and trained in
emergency response to enable them to co-ordinate evacuation activities in case of emergency.
Management Response
Personnel manning the Data Centre will be trained on how to respond in case of fire
outbreak or other emergencies.
Fire Marshals or emergency response teams will be appointed, equipped and trained in
emergency response to enable them to co-ordinate evacuation activities in case of
emergency. This will be done in the 2025 Budget year.
2.3
Outsourcing and Internal Service Level Agreements (SLA)
Finding
For the third year running, both internal and outsourcing SLAs were not available for audit
inspection. As a result, I was unable to confirm whether;
•
PFMS was getting value for money from suppliers of products and services such as
hardware, software, and networking infrastructure.
•
Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs) were satisfied with PFMS's service
levels.
This was against best practice which states that security mechanisms, service levels and
management requirements of all network, hardware and software services should be identified
and included in service level agreements, whether these services are provided in-house or
outsourced. The SLAs should also cover issues of liability, reliability of services and response
times for the provision of services.

Risks/Implications

In the absence of Outsourcing SLAs, suppliers and partners may not be held liable for failing
to meet their service obligations.

MDAs' service delivery by ICT units may be compromised without Internal SLAs.

Recommendation

Service-level agreements should be established with vendors and MDAs in order to evaluate
and improve service delivery.

88

Management Response

Service Level Agreements will be established with vendors and MDAs in order to
evaluate and improve service delivery. This will be done by the second quarter of 2025.
3     CHANGE MANAGEMENT
3.1
Change Management Policy and Procedures
Findings
The PFMS Information Security Policy submitted for audit had provisions for change
management such as approval, evaluation and recording of changes, the scope was limited
because it did not include provisions for migration of program changes and emergency change
procedures.
This was contrary to Best Practice which states that changes to the organisation, business
processes, information processing facilities and systems that affect information security should
be controlled, including a provision of an emergency change process to enable quick and
controlled implementation of changes needed to resolve an incident.
Risk/Implication
The integrity of data and processing may be compromised if Change Management Policy and
Emergency Change Procedures are not in place.
Recommendation
Management should establish and approve a Change Management Policy Document that
includes migration of program changes and emergency changes.
Management Response
The observation is noted, management will review in the first quarter of 2025, the
existing Change Management Policy Document to include migration of program
changes and emergency changes.
4       EXPENDITURE BUSINESS CYCLE
4.1
Goods Receipt/Invoice Receipt (GR/IR) Clearing Account
Finding
The Goods Receipt or Invoice Receipt (GR/IR) suspense account is used to ensure that the
goods received correspond to the amounts invoiced by vendors for those goods. For the third
year in a row, I observed uncleared transactions totaling ZWL$109 625 206 695 in the GR/IR
suspense accounts from a sample of ten (10) ministries and departments. Unreconciled entries
included duplicated supplier invoices, goods receipts with no matching supplier invoices,
supplier invoices with no matching goods receipts, and invoiced quantities greater than
quantities received.
Risks/Implications
Uncleared items in the GR/IR account may facilitate unauthorised transactions.

Financial statements may be misstated if GR/IR mismatches are not timeously resolved.
89

Recommendations

Ministries, Departments and Agencies should investigate all uncleared transactions.

MDAs should conduct regular reconciliations of GR/IR suspense accounts to identify and
address discrepancies in time.

The Ministry of Finance should monitor the GR/IR accounts to ensure that they are cleared

Management Response
We take note of this matter and it is critical in the new era of reporting under IPSAS to
ensure this account is cleared. We will continue to advise MDAs to clear this account.

POVERTY ALLEVIATION PROJECT: MINISTRY OF WOMEN AFFAIRS


1.1
Monitoring and Evaluation

Finding

The Government of Zimbabwe entered into a loan agreement of US$7.6 million with OPEC
Fund for International Development (OFID) on August 23, 2016 for the Poverty Alleviation
Project. The objective of the project was to improve access of beneficiary households to
enhanced socio-economic services and income-generating opportunities. The Ministry of
Women Affairs, Gender and Enterprises Development served as the Implementing Agent for
the project responsible for training of beneficiaries, monitoring and evaluation of the projects
in all the provinces.

During my audit in November 2023, the Ministry was not carrying out monitoring and evaluation
of twenty-four (24) Poverty Alleviation financed projects, in Masvingo, Bulawayo and
Manicaland. The provinces indicated that they did not have information of the beneficiaries and
the projects. The beneficiary information was made available when my audit was underway.
Consequently, beneficiaries embarked on projects without adequate training and guidance
leading to failure of projects to take off, implementation as expected and misuse of the project
funds.

For instance, Bukuso Cooperative received US$50 000 to boast their animal husbandry
projects, namely cattle and goat fattening, poultry and fish farming as well as piggery. An
inspection of project site revealed that piggery, cattle fattening, fish and goat projects were
abandoned due to lack of knowledge by members of the cooperative and technical advice from
103

the Ministry Officials.

Risk/ Implication

Without regular monitoring and evaluation, financial resources may not be used for the
intended purpose and the objective of the project may not be achieved.

Recommendation

The Public Debt Management Office should ensure that the Ministry of Women Affairs and
Community Development has information relating to project beneficiaries and that regular
monitoring and evaluation is performed.

Management Response

The Provincial Development Officer for Masvingo province and Business Development
Officer for Mwenezi district who had project information resigned from employment in
2020. In addition, even if the funds to monitor were available from the project, the
number of days to cover all projects was controlled to minimize the budget. There was
no complementary budget from the Ministry to support monitoring of these project
activities. Motor vehicles were also a challenge since most of these projects were far
from the offices.

1.2
Training of beneficiaries

Findings

Audit noted that, for all the twenty-four (24) projects sampled out and visited in November
2023, the beneficiaries were not trained in project management and record keeping before
receiving funding. This was due to lack of coordination between the project implementing team
at Head office and the Provincial Offices responsible for training and monitoring of projects.
This resulted in non-maintenance of records to account for funds provided and project failures.

For instance, in Masvingo province, Mujo holdings was given US$18 000 to start a gold mill
but the project was abandoned. Ark life Private limited was given US$30 000 to start a broiler
project which failed to take off. Moriah Cattle Fattening was given US$40 000 to start the
project. OFID Poverty Alleviation Project- Disbursement Modalities (2017), require that
selected beneficiaries should attend an on-site technical training (where necessary) before
receiving funding.

Risk/Implication

Expenditure could be incurred for projects that have been abandoned resulting in fruitless
expenditure.

Recommendations

The Public Debt Management Office should provide training to beneficiaries before allocating
loans.

Management Response

The observation is noted. The Ministry will improve on both business management and
technical training of beneficiaries.

 MINISTRY OF LANDS, AGRICULTURE, FISHERIES, WATER AND RURAL

DEVELOPMENT: SMALLHOLDER IRRIGATION PROJECT (SIRP): 2019-2020

2.1
Contractual Obligations

Findings

Three (3) out of sixteen (16) irrigation projects visited in Masvingo, Manicaland and
Matabeleland South had progress of work by contractors slowed down due to late payments

Matabeleland, progress was stalled at Rustlers Gorge Irrigation Scheme, due to non-payment
of the contractor.

Further, an audit inspection of Romsley Irrigation scheme in Manicaland province on
November 15, 2023 revealed that construction works at lot 2 lagged behind because the
contractor could not discharge his obligation of blasting stones for canal construction on an
18-kilometer stretch due to lack of capacity. At Insukamini Irrigation scheme, the contractor left
the construction site without carrying out land levelling which was part of the scope of works
despite being paid in full.

Risks/Implications

Incomplete projects and compromised service delivery.

The objective of food security through smallholder irrigation projects might not be realized if
projects are left incomplete.

Recommendation

The Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) should ensure that the Ministry of Lands,
Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Rural development as the implementing partner pays
contractors timeously for completed works in order to allow them to meet the running costs

Management Response

The observation is noted. The contractor at Rustlers Irrigation was paid all the

boreholes (well points). He has failed to upgrade the existing submersible pumps. He is

2.2    Back-up Power

Finding

Finding

An inspection of Ramsey Irrigation scheme revealed that more than 50% of the land had not
been cleared. The department of Irrigation had inadequate land clearing equipment. PSIP

Overnight Storage Dams
Findings

An inspection of Ramsey Irrigation scheme showed that construction work had not started on
two (2) overnight dams due to non-availability of adequate equipment and financial resources

Risks/Implications

Land earmarked for irrigation may remain unutilized if overnight storage dams are not

The Public Debt Management Office should engage the Department of Irrigation so that the

Findings

is used through drawdowns by the Ministry. Royalties from CBCA Programme had no
independent PFMS ledger account, it was being accounted for in the Import and Export fees
ledger account.

The Revenue Received in form of CBCA Royalties reported was US$3 345 981 while invoices

amounts due.

Misclassification of revenue resulting in understatement of revenue reported.
Recommendations

The Ministry should invoice contractors timeously as per the agreement.

Variances should be investigated and adjustments should be made in the ledgers and the
returns.

 Finding

The cash and cash equivalence figure on the consolidated statement of financial position
amounted to ZWL$3 121 043 159 for the year 2023 while the cash flow statement closing cash

Suspense

 Finding

The statement of financial position for the year ended December 31, 2023 had an imbalance
(Suspense) amounting to ZWL$175 491 013. I was not furnished with a satisfactory

(vi) Submission of Receipt Books and Security Items Register

 Findings

I was not provided with the security items register to verify whether the receipt books used to

Risk/Implication

Fraudulent activities may go undetected in the absence of security items register.

(ii)
Land Compensation

Finding

Land compensation payments amounting to ZWL$2 244 132 725 disclosed in the financial
statements were not supported. There were no valuation reports produced for each farm
neither were the minutes of the Land compensation committee approval of the property
valuations. Therefore, the expenditure on compensation to the farmers could not be validated

Deed. When audits were carried out, negotiations on valuation rates and other
parameters were still ongoing between the Government and Farmers. Agreements were
reached and the new valuation rates were adopted and effected on valuation reports.
Valuation reports are now available and minutes of the compensation committee where
fixing of values was undertaken can be availed at your request.

It is on the basis of these valuation reports and Compensation Committee resolutions
that compensation payments are now being done, starting January 1, 2024.

Finding

reconciliations between the SSB wage bill and compensation of employee costs shown in the

Payments may be made to non-existent employees and errors in records remain undetected.

I have audited the financial statements of the Meteorological Services Fund for the years ended
December 31, 2020 to 2023 and I issued an adverse opinion for the four (4) years.

Adverse Opinion

In my opinion, because of the significance of the matters described in the Basis for Adverse
Opinion section of my report, the financial statements do not present fairly the financial position
of the Meteorological Services Fund as at December 31, 2023, and its financial performance
and its cash flows for the year then ended in accordance with the Public Finance Management
Act [Chapter 22:19] and other relevant Statutory Instruments.

Basis for Adverse Opinion

(i)
Conversion of Foreign Exchange Transactions

Finding

In 2023, management used the exchange rate of the last day of each month to convert monthly
foreign currency transactions reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income instead of
converting using exchange rate applicable on the date of the transaction. For the period 2020
to 2022 average exchange rate was used to convert foreign exchange transactions instead of
converting using exchange rates applicable on the date of the transactions. The Statement of
Financial Position balances were converted using the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe Ask Rate
instead of the Mid-Rate for the year 2020 to 2022.

Risk/Implication

Misstatement of financial statements.


167

Recommendation

Management should ensure that they convert foreign denominated accounts into the
presentation currency using the rates at the date of transaction for the Statement of
Comprehensive Income components and the closing rate for the year for the Statement of
Financial Position.

Management Response

The observation has been noted. Going forward, the Fund will ensure compliance with
appropriate International Accounting Standards and use the exchange rate applicable.

While management acknowledge the finding, it should be noted that for revenues or
enroute fees, monthly exchange rates were used as disclosed in the financial
statements, hence using daily exchange rates for expenses violates or compromises
accounting principles such as consistency and matching.

Evaluation of Management Response

Using exchange rates applicable on the date of the transactions does not violate any
accounting principles, rather it upholds the standard.

(ii)
Foreign Exchange Gain

Finding

There was no evidence supporting how management had calculated or determined the Foreign
Exchange Gains of ZWL$735 820 632 for 2023, (2022: ZWL$203 284 989),
(2021: ZWL$5 601 179) and (2020: ZWL$8 496 400) reported in the Statements of
Comprehensive Income. The accuracy of the amounts could not be confirmed in the absence
of the supporting documentation showing how the exchange gains were determined.

Risk/Implication

The financial statements could have been misstated.

Recommendation

Management should provide the supporting documentation showing how the exchange gains
were determined.

Management Response

The end of year exchange rate was used during the preparation of Financial Statements
instead of the rate on the transaction date. This resulted in exchange rate gain. The
anomaly will be corrected.

The foreign exchange gains were based on matching the monthly US$ conversions
using closing monthly spot rates. These were then summed up to attain the year’s profit
in local currency compared with the US$ profit on the Statement of Comprehensive
Income, that was converted using closing rate.




168

Evaluation of Management Response

Management response is acknowledged. However, the above-mentioned calculations were
not availed for audit.

GOVERNANCE ISSUES

1.1    Segregation of Duties in the Fuel Management Process

Finding

There was no segregation of duties in the fuel management process for the period 2020 to
2023. The same officer was responsible for requesting the purchase of fuel and signing for the
fuel request, issuing the fuel coupons and recording them in the fuel register. This was contrary
to Section 158(2) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 which
states that an Accounting Officer shall ensure that there is segregation of duties. As a result,
no checks and balances were being carried out.

Risk/Implication

Errors may not be picked as all the tasks are done by the same person and fuel coupons may
be misappropriated.

Recommendation

Management should ensure that there is segregation of duties. This will minimise errors and
facilitate checks and controls.

Management Response

During the period under review, there was a shortage of staff. However, interviews were
held and some of the posts have been filled. This will improve our internal controls.

1.2    Management Committee

Finding

The Management Committee met once on November 3, 2023, instead of at least four (4) times
per year as stipulated in Section 3 of the Meteorological Service Fund Constitution. The
Management Committee performs the oversight duties of the Fund.

Risk/Implication

The efficient and effective operation of the Fund may be compromised when the Management
Committee does not meet regularly.



175

Recommendation

The Management Committee should meet as per the regulations.

Management Response

We have taken note of the observation and in future we are going to adhere to the
recommendation and act accordingly.

1.3    Payments Made Based on Proforma Invoices or Quotations

Finding

I noted that payments for Communication Supplies and Services and Contributions and
Subscriptions were made based on proforma invoices or quotations. The total value of the
payments was ZWL$2 360 493 and US$5 049 for the period 2020 to 2022. This was in violation
of section 59(2) (c) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 which
states that on no account shall a payment be made on the basis of a quotation only but submit
an original invoice for the amount claimed and this shall be attached to the voucher.

Risk/Implication

There may be overpayments for goods and services when proforma invoices/quotations are
used.

Recommendation

Management should ensure that all payments are made based on original invoices in order to
reduce risks associated with overpayments.

Management Response

The observation is noted. However, this has been rectified and original invoices have
been collected.

Management response is appreciated. However, the original invoices were not submitted for
evaluation.

Finding

Bank reconciliations for 2023, 2022, 2021 and 2020 were not being performed on a monthly
basis for both ZWL$ and US$ Bank Accounts. This was in contravention of Section 6.1.7 of
the Accounting Procedures Manual which requires the senior accountant to reconcile all bank
accounts monthly.

Fraud and errors may not be detected in time.

3.1
Valuation of Properties

 Findings

In determining compensation amounts for properties affected by the Trabablas (Mbudzi)
Interchange Project, the Ministry engaged the services of three professional property valuers
for the calculation of an average value as compensation amount. Despite the prescribed
methodology of averaging the property values determined by the three (3) valuers, I noted
discrepancies in compensation amounts offered to property owners.

In some instances, the highest value among the three (3) valuations was adopted as the
compensation amount, deviating from the established practice of averaging the three property
amounts. The total variance between the amount offered and that derived from the average
amounted to ZWL$24 315 185 226 (US$3 983 014). Selection of the highest valuated amount
as the compensation raises concerns about the objectivity and fairness of the compensation
process. This approach disregards the purpose of engaging multiple valuers to mitigate bias
whilst ensuring that a balanced assessment of property values is maintained throughout the
entire process.

Risk/Implication

The Ministry could have been prejudiced of public funds as a result of deviation from the
standard procedure.

Recommendation

The Ministry should adhere to the set standard practice of determining the compensation
amount using the average rate. Corrective action should be taken to address the anomaly.

Management Response

The two (2) private valuers were contracted and paid for the services rendered to the
Ministry.  The reports from the two private valuers were requested so that comparisons
could be made for value for money to be compared, since private valuers are
192

professionals in the industry of disposing properties. Variance and inconsistencies in
valuation were caused by the property owners who refused to accept the offer based
on average and claimed that they only accept the offer from Local Government and
Public works.

3.2
Registration of Land expropriated for Trabablas (Mbudzi) Interchange

       Finding

The Ministry did not provide evidence which shows notification to the Registrar of Deeds of the
expropriated land for Trabablas (Mbudzi) Interchange so that no other transactions are done
on the property. This was contrary to Section 10 (1) of Land Acquisition Act [Chapter 20:10],
which states that upon the ownership of any land being vested in an acquiring authority, the
acquiring authority shall, as soon as practicable thereafter, notify the Registrar of Deeds in
writing of that fact.

                   Risk/Implication

The property owners could sell the properties or obtain mortgages using the title deeds giving
rise to potential legal challenges with the ownership of the properties.

                   Recommendation

The Ministry should comply with the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act [Chapter 20:10]   to
safeguard its interests.

                   Management Response

The compensation of property owners is not yet complete. The majority of the affected
property owners are yet to receive full compensation.  It is against this background that
the Ministry could not ask the affected property owners to relinquish the Title Deeds as
this will cause legal disputes.

The process of notifying Registrar of Deeds is done after actual construction of the
project. The Ministry’s survey team will go on site, measure the portion of the land
previously occupied by the affected property owners and new diagrams will be
produced and that information is submitted to the Registrar of Deeds.

                   Evaluation of Management Response

Management response indicates that the notification to the Registrar of Deeds is done after
the completion of the construction project. While this approach could align with the Ministry's
operational procedures, it is essential to alert the Deeds Office of the development to ensure
that the property owners would not sell the properties or obtain mortgages using the title deeds
of the properties under sale.

The expenditure ledgers showed that there were open items amounting to ZWG366 349 742

• Some of them needs thorough scrutiny before reversal since there was a lot of

3.2     Maintenance of Government Buildings

Findings

The Public Works Department is charged with ownership of all Government buildings and
maintenance.

Programme 4 (Construction, Maintenance and Management of Public Buildings) was allocated
a total of ZWG759 155 951 as a budget estimate during the year under review. However, there
was no budget allocation for maintenance programmes.  As a result, there was no structured
maintenance of Government buildings due to lack of budgetary support.

217

Section 36 (1) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 states that the
Accounting Officer shall monitor the performance of the budget regularly to ensure delivery of
expected results and to address any deviations from the ministry’s targets.

Risks/Implications

Failure to adhere to the Physical Infrastructure and Construction Works budgeted amounts by
all Ministries may cause deterioration of the Government Buildings in the long run.

Recommendations

The Ministry should create a database of all repairs and maintenance works requests executed
and outstanding requests and ensure allocations for repairs and maintenance for all
Government buildings are utilized strictly for that purpose.

Management Response

There was very little maintenance of Government Buildings during the year 2024 and
this was as a result of tight budgetary constraints. However, the Ministry has since
requested Treasury to avail Officials from the Accountant General’s Department and
Recurrent Expenditure during the period 5 to 16 May 2025 for a tour to familiarize and
appreciate the need for maintenance of Government Buildings in various Provinces.

4       MANAGEMENT OF ASSETS

4.1    Master Assets Register

Finding

The Ministry did not maintain a Master assets register. I was not able to ascertain how the
assets were accounted for in the absence of the above master assets register. Section 100 (1)
of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions) 2019, requires the Accounting
Officers to ensure that all public assets are recorded promptly and accurately in the appropriate
manual registers. The assets should also be captured immediately on the PFMS system.

Risk/Implication

The absence of the Master assets register could expose them to misuse and misappropriation.

Recommendation

The Ministry should ensure that a master assets register is put in place to safeguard the
Ministry’s assets.

Management Response

The record of all assets procured through the system since 2009 are available in the
system and the values are a challenge because of the cash accounting policy that was
being used during that time. Updating of the manual master asset register is currently
in progress and the missing values and other details will be extracted from the available
excel sheet compiled for IPSAS.


218

4.2    Donated Vehicles

Findings

Six (6) donated vehicles were not recorded in the donation and vehicle registers. Section 103
(14) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 requires the Accounting
Officers to ensure that a vehicle register detailing the make, model, engine and chassis number
is maintained for Government vehicles under their control.

Furthermore, a sample of the vehicles inspected revealed that some of the vehicles did not
have log books.

Risks/Implications

Vehicles not recorded in the vehicle register may be exposed to misuse and misappropriation.

The motor vehicles may be used for purposes not related to the Ministry ‘s business resulting
in accelerated wear and tear and high maintenance costs.

Recommendation

Accounting Officers should make sure that vehicle registers are maintained and updated.

Management Response

The donated vehicles were recorded in the donations register and the vehicle register
availed to audit. The Ministry will ensure that each vehicle has a log book and reminder
will be issued to all users except personal issue vehicles to complete the log books for
every trip undertaken in line with regulations. The transport officer will also ensure
monthly returns are submitted and carry out reconciliation for each vehicle.

Evaluation of Management Response

The management response is appreciated. Two (2) vehicles were recorded in the donations
register leaving six (6) unrecorded. Further, all donated vehicles should be recorded in the
donations register as well as the vehicle register.

I have audited the financial statements of the Ministry of Health and Child Care for the year
ended December 31, 2024 and I issued an adverse opinion.

Adverse Opinion

In my opinion, because of the significance of the matters discussed in the Basis for Adverse
Opinion section of my report, the financial statements do not present fairly, the state of affairs
of the Ministry of Health and Child Care as at December 31, 2024, in accordance with the
Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19] and other relevant Statutory Instruments.

Basis for Adverse Opinion

(i)     Direct Payments
Findings
There was an unexplained variance of US$3 135 050 between an amount of US$22 656 013
disclosed on the Treasury Direct Payments schedule and the Direct payment notification letters
of US$19 520 963 submitted by the Ministry for audit. Further, the direct payments were not
accounted for through the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) and were not
disclosed in the Appropriation Account. As a result, the total expenditure disclosed in the PFMS
and Appropriation Account was misstated by US$19 520 963.

The supporting documents for the direct payments such as payment vouchers, invoices and
goods receipt notes were not availed for audit. Therefore, I could not ascertain whether the
goods and services paid for were received and related to the Ministry.
 Risks/Implications
The expenditure disclosed in the Appropriation Account and PFMS could be materially
understated.
Expenditure may be incurred for goods and services not received by the Ministry.

235

Recommendations
Management should follow up with Treasury to avail the Direct payment notification letters and
ensure that the variance of US$3 135 050 is addressed.
The Ministry should engage Treasury to ensure that the direct payments are regularised in the
PFMS. In addition, the supporting documents for payments made should be availed for audit.
Management Response
The Ministry is in the process of conducting reconciliations of direct payments with
Treasury. Treasury has been engaged for confirmation of amounts paid on behalf of the
Ministry and to ensure that all expenditure is recorded.

(ii)     Reconciliation of Appropriation Account Expenditure

Finding
The Appropriation Account disclosed total expenditure of ZWG7 453 988 622, the PFMS Funds
Management report had expenditure of ZWG7 453 426 221 whilst the Sub-Paymaster General
(Sub-PMG) Account reconciliation statement reflected ZWG875 786 578. Under normal
circumstances, the expenditure amount should be the same in the three (3) records or a
reconciliation should be provided when they are different. I could not therefore, validate the
accuracy of expenditure reported in the Ministry’s Appropriation Account.
Risk/Implication
The total expenditure reported in the Appropriation Account could be misstated.
Recommendation
Management should investigate and reconcile the variances, ensuring that all expenditure is
accurately disclosed in the Appropriation Account.
Management Response

The audit finding is noted. The reconciliation between the Sub-PMG and PFMS Funds
Management Report is being re-performed to ensure compliance.

(iii) Clearance of Open Items

Findings

The Ministry had uncleared transactions of ZWL$178 500 300 943 in the PFMS Cash Book
and Sub-Paymaster General transfers. The uncleared items represented transactions
processed in the PFMS that had not been funded and reversed as at December 31, 2024.
Therefore, the expenditure disclosed in the Appropriation Account was inaccurate as the
unfunded amounts were reflected as expenditure in the PFM System.

In addition, the uncleared transactions in the Goods Receipt/Invoice Receipt Clearing Account
of ZWG8 243 620 631 represent the difference between the value of invoiced goods and the
goods received implying that there were goods and services procured that may not have been
delivered at year end. Treasury Circular Number 1 of 2025 requires all uncleared transactions
in the system to be cleared before preparing annual returns and financial statements to ensure
completeness and alignment.



236

       Risk/Implication

 The expenditure disclosed in the Appropriation Account could be inaccurate as the unfunded
amounts may be reflected as expenditure in the PFM System while goods and services
procured may not have been delivered at year end.
Recommendation

The Ministry should ensure that all outstanding open items are investigated and resolved on
time and that all unfunded payment runs are reversed.

Management Response
The audit observation is noted. The Ministry has engaged Ministry of Finance, Economic
Development and Investment Promotion to open the 13th period to enable clearance of
the open items.

(iv)  Compensation of Employees

Finding

 The Appropriation Account had total compensation of employee costs of ZWG4 852 692 234
while the Salary Services Bureau (SSB) Wage bill report showed ZWG4 669 595 770 resulting
in a variance of ZWG183 096 464.  There was no evidence that monthly reconciliations were
performed as required by Treasury Circular B/1/88 June 5, 2018. As a result, I could not
validate the accuracy of employment costs disclosed in the financial statements.

Risk/Implication

The compensation of employee costs reported for the year under review may be misstated.
Recommendation

Management should ensure that compensation of employee costs billed by SSB are reconciled
monthly against expenditure figures shown in the PFMS ledgers and any variance should be
investigated.

Management Response

The observation is noted. The variance primarily stems from US$ denominated bonuses
that were not recorded in December 2024 as the wage bill was not received. Additionally,
management is reviewing further minor discrepancies of ZWG455 073 for May 2024,
ZWG1 551 for June 2024 and ZWG559 for November 2024.

(v)
Completeness of Revenue Received

Findings
The Revenue Received return showed total revenue of ZWG807 319 while the supporting
PFMS General Ledger showed ZWG272 555 resulting in an unreconciled variance of
ZWG534 764. At the time of concluding the audit in April 2025, the Ministry was in the process
of uploading 2024 receipts onto the PFMS and indicated that this was due to technical
challenges encountered during the transition to the new PFMS platform in 2024.
237

Further, Manicaland and Matabeleland South Provinces submitted revenue returns which had
ZWL$121 347 719 and US$14 817 respectively that were not converted to ZWG. As a result
of non-conversion to ZWG, the revenue received reported was inaccurate.
Risk/Implication

The Revenue received may be incomplete and understated.

Recommendation

Management should investigate, rectify the variances and convert the revenue received from
ZWL$ to ZWG.

Management Response

The observation is noted. The amount of ZWG270 000 is accrued revenue raised from
penalties of late notification of resignation by staff members. It was not included on the
revenue return as the financial statements are prepared on cash basis. The
reconciliation of revenue received has now been submitted for audit.

For the year under review, five (5) provinces collected revenue for the exchequer
account and receipted in the PFMS. The remaining five (5) provinces did not collect any
revenue for the exchequer account as there were no services provided.

Evaluation of Management Response

The management response is noted. However, under cash basis accounting, revenue is
recognized when cash is received. Therefore, the amount of ZWG270 000 should be
accounted for in 2024 when it was received.

The issue of conversion of revenue from ZWL$ and US$ to ZWG was not addressed.

(vi) Outstanding Disallowances

Finding

The Statement of Outstanding Advances including Disallowances showed a balance of
ZWG849 167 which differed from the PFMS figure of ZWG2 535 279, resulting in an
unreconciled variance of ZWG1 686 112. At the time of concluding the audit on April, 30, 2025
the Ministry was still posting 2024 disallowances into the PFMS. Therefore, I could not confirm
with certainty the accuracy of the Outstanding Disallowance figure disclosed.

Risk/Implication

The supporting statements to the Appropriation Account may be misstated.

Recommendation

The Ministry should timely upload information onto the PFMS and a reconciliation between the
figures on the Disallowance return and PFMS General Ledger should be performed.

Management Response

The audit observation is noted. The variance noted was due to system downtime and
delays in the configuration of the ZWG Client 600 platform. Furthermore, the Ministry
238

experienced high levels of late notification of terminations and resignations. As a result,
processing and invoicing of the 2024 Disallowances was only initiated during the 13th
period in 2025. The process is ongoing and the Ministry will ensure alignment between
the Disallowance Return and the General Ledger.

GOVERNANCE ISSUES

Budget Utilisation

Finding

The Ministry had a budget allocation of ZWG9 483 013 455. However actual funding for

Health service delivery may be compromised due to inadequate funding.
The accumulation of arrears if left unattended to, negatively impacts on Government

The Ministry should continue lobbying for the release of funding by Treasury to enable

Filling of Vacant Posts

Finding

For the fifth year running, the Ministry had twenty (20) managerial vacant posts in the Finance,

Evidence supporting the requests and follow-ups made to the relevant authorities to fill in the

Board and Treasury.

Risks/Implications

Existence of too many vacant positions affects productivity there by compromising service
delivery.

There may be inadequate segregation of duties resulting in self-review of work and errors not

Management should continuously make requests and follow ups to the Health Service Board

 The Ministry submitted an unapproved Annual Operational Plan for audit. The Plan did not

Resource management, monitoring of progress and risk management may not be effectively

I have audited the financial statements of the Health Services Fund for the year ended
December 31, 2023 and I issued an adverse opinion.

Adverse Opinion

In my opinion, because of the significance of the matters discussed in the Basis for Adverse
Opinion section of my report, the financial statements do not present fairly the financial position
of the Health Services Fund as at December 31, 2023, its financial performance and its cash
flows for the year then ended in accordance with the Public Finance Management Act
[Chapter 22:19] and other relevant Statutory Instruments.

Basis for Adverse Opinion

(i)
Basis for Preparation of Financial Statements

Finding

The Fund did not comply with a specific acceptable financial reporting framework in preparation
of the financial statements. The financial statements were prepared using both the cash and
accrual accounting basis in line with the Fund’s Financial and Accounting Manual. There was
no clear indication of which components were reported on cash or accrual basis. Section 116
(5) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 requires Fund financial
statements to be prepared on an accrual basis. As a result, the financial statements could be
misstated.

Risk/Implication

Understandability and reliability of financial statements may be compromised.

245

Recommendation

The Ministry should amend its Financial and Accounting Procedures Manual for the Health
Services Fund (HSF) and come out with a clear basis for preparing financial statements.

Management Response

The Ministry is in the process of amending the Financial and Accounting Procedures
Manual for the HSF and align the reporting framework with IPSAS accrual.

(ii)  Bank Balance

Finding

For the second year running, I could not validate with certainty the completeness of the
consolidated cash at bank balance of ZWL$9 753 608 148. Out of eighty-eight (88) health
institutions, ten (10) did not submit bank statements and certificates of balance to support the
cash at bank balance figure. The Ministry did not have a mechanism in place such as a register
to confirm whether all the health institutions under the Health Services Fund had submitted
their financial statements and relevant supporting documents for consolidation.  As a result,
the accuracy of the bank balance could not be confirmed with certainty.

                  Risk/Implication

Some balances could be omitted resulting in material misstatement of the consolidated
financial statements.

Recommendation

Management should put in place a mechanism to enable confirmation of all cash and bank
balances disclosed in the financial statements.

Management Response

 The observation is noted. The bank statements and certificates for seventy-eight (78)
health institutions were availed for the audit.

(iii) Other Income

Findings

Included in the Other Income amount of ZWL$4 504 382 651 reported in the Statement of
Comprehensive Income is an amount of ZWL$4 367 808 870 relating to foreign exchange rate
gains on income and expenditure transactions. However, the income and expense
transactions were translated using the closing rate at the balance sheet date instead of the
exchange rates on the dates of transacting.

In addition, the translation was effected on the 2022 closing Accumulated Fund figure instead
of the individual income and expenses accounts. Section 34.2.4(a) of the Financial and
Accounting Procedures Manual for the Health Service Fund requires foreign currency
transactions to be translated at the official exchange rate on the date of the transaction. As a
result, the accuracy of the exchange rate gain could not be confirmed with certainty.

Further, the Fund did not include an explanation and breakdown of the remaining balance of
the Other Income of ZWL$136 573 781. The accuracy of the Other Income reported in the
246

financial statements could not therefore be ascertained.

Risk/Implication

Financial statements could be misstated.

Recommendations

The Ministry should use the foreign exchange rate at the date of transaction in compliance with
the regulations.


Management should ensure that comprehensive notes are provided to support figures
disclosed in the financial statements.

Management Response

The observation is noted. A reconciliation of exchange differences was shared on
October 14, 2024. Going forward, the Ministry will adhere to Section 34.2.4 (a) of the
Financial and Accounting Procedures Manual in preparation of financial statements.

Evaluation of Management Response

Management response is acknowledged. The issue of the misstated exchange rate gain was
not addressed and the breakdown of the remaining balance of Other Income was not availed.

(iv) Variances Between Consolidated and Provincial Financial Statements Figures

Findings

Audit noted variances of ZWL$21 852 837 on income, ZWL$2 472 571 on expenditure and
ZWL$21 852 837 on cash at bank between figures disclosed in the consolidated financial
statements and Masvingo provincial financial statements. Under normal circumstances the
figures reported in the provincial financial statements should be the same as those reported in
the consolidated financial statements.

Additionally, a variance of ZWL$2 190 733 and US$277 between the income figures reported
in the financial statements and the receipts issued by the Government Analyst Laboratory
(GAL) was noted. There was no evidence of maintenance of revenue ledgers to ensure that
all revenue transactions were correctly recorded as required by Section 9.3 of the Financial
and Accounting Procedures Manual for the Health Service Fund. As a result, of the uncorrected
variances, the reliability and accuracy of the financial statements could be compromised.

Risk/Implication

Expenditure and revenue figures may be misstated.
Recommendations
Management should timely investigate variances and make the necessary adjustments before
submission of financial statements for audit.

Proper accounting records including relevant ledgers should be maintained.

247

Management Response
Head Office: An incorrect excel file for the consolidated return was erroneously
forwarded to auditors. The correct return that was used for final consolidation had
matching figures. The correct financial statements have now been shared with the
auditors.
GAL: The maintenance of ledgers is a function of the Accounting Assistant whose post
is currently vacant. Management commits to maintain appropriate, up to date and
relevant ledgers for the HSF.
Evaluation of Management Response

Management response is acknowledged, however, at the time of concluding the audit on
January 14, 2025, Head Office had not shared the correct financial statements for Masvingo.

(v)
Cash Withdrawals and Unsupported Expenditure

Findings

Gweru Provincial hospital made cash withdrawals totalling US$29 111 between September
20, 2023 and October 6, 2023, to cover the procurement cost of US$24 000 for the autoclave
machine and traveling costs of US$1 936 to South Africa. The hospital submitted for audit
supporting documents for payments of US$22 471 made to the supplier for the autoclave
machine and travel costs of US$ 1 936. Evidence of how the balance of US$4 704 was utilised
was not availed for audit. I could not therefore, confirm whether all the cash withdrawn was
used for the intended purpose.
Further, on May 19, 2023, Gweru Provincial Hospital withdrew cash amounting to US$4 667
from the bank for the purpose of paying various suppliers of goods and services. Payment
vouchers amounting to US$4 540 were availed to support how the cash was utilised however,
an amount of US$127 remained unsupported. In addition, the payments were processed
between March 21, 2023 and May 8, 2023 prior to the cash withdrawal date. The hospital did
not maintain a cash register to assist in tracking cash payments. Therefore, I could not confirm
with certainty whether the payment vouchers availed were the appropriate supporting
documents for the amount withdrawn.  As a result, the credibility of the expenditure disclosed
in the financial statements could be compromised.
Risks/Implications
Public funds may not be used for intended purpose.

Fraudulent activities may be perpetrated if registers are not maintained to account for all
withdrawals and usage of the money.

Recommendations

Hospital management should submit proof of payments and receipts for audit as evidence of
how the cash withdrawals were utilized.

The hospital should have adequate safeguards such as maintenance of a cash register for all
cash payments.

Cash withdrawals should be avoided and payments should be done through the Electronic
Funds Transfer system.
248

Management Response

All supporting documents for the noted transactions are in place and have now been
availed to the auditors.

Evaluation of Management Response

Management response is acknowledged. However, evidence of how the balances of $4 704
and US$127 on the cash withdrawals for the procurement of the autoclave machine and
payments to various suppliers were utilised was not availed for audit. There was no evidence
that the amount was subsequently banked.

(vi) Under Banking

Finding

Out of a total of US$376 764 receipted at Gweru Provincial Hospital between January and
December 2023, US$338 213 was banked resulting in failure to account for US$38 551. As a
result of the under banking, I could not confirm with certainty the completeness of the revenue
disclosed in the financial statements.

Risk/Implication

Inaccurate balances may be reported in the financial statements.

Recommendation

An independent senior officer should regularly review the cash management records to ensure
that monies are timely banked and intact.  Any variations to the banking period should be
supported by the Accounting Officer’s approval.

Management Response

Management has noted the audit observation in relation to receipting and cash
management. Measures have now been put in place to ensure the recommendations are
followed.

Evaluation of Management Response

The management response is acknowledged. However, the issue of unaccounted receipts of
US$38 551 was not responded to.

(vii)   Unearned Revenue

Finding

The Ministry disclosed unearned revenue amounting to ZWL$38 860 659 under current
liabilities. However, no supporting documents were availed for audit inspection. Consequently,
I could not validate the figure or confirm the services paid for but not rendered. The current
liabilities could be overstated.

Risk/Implication

The current liabilities disclosed in the financial statements may be misstated.
249

Recommendation
Management should carry out an investigation to determine the source of the figure and update
the auditors.

Management Response

A reconciliation of the unearned revenue was availed for audit inspection.

Evaluation of Management Response

The management response is acknowledged. The reconciliation availed was a breakdown of
the unearned revenue figure for three (3) provinces and one (1) health institution and did not
show details of the services paid for in advance to facilitate confirmation.

Below are other issues noted during the audit:

1
GOVERNANCE ISSUES

1.1
Bank Reconciliations

Findings

Audit noted that Chinhoyi Provincial Hospital had health fees receipts amounting to
ZWL$1 147 382 collected through Point of Sale (POS), Ecocash platform, and direct bank
deposits which were receipted after six months.

In addition, the Government Analyst Laboratory (GAL) took more than 180 days to investigate
and clear direct deposits of US$1 658 and ZWL$121 134. There was no evidence of daily and
