I have audited the financial statements of the School Services Fund for the year ended
December 31, 2023 and I issued an adverse opinion.

Adverse Opinion

In my opinion, because of the significance of the matters discussed in the Basis for Adverse
Opinion section of my report, the financial statements do not present fairly the financial position
of the School Services Fund as at December 31, 2023, its financial performance and its cash
flows for the year then ended in accordance with the Public Finance Management Act
[Chapter 22:19] and other relevant Statutory Instruments.

Basis for Adverse Opinion

(i)      Maintenance of Accounting Records
Finding
The School Services Fund’s (SSF) management did not maintain the required ledger accounts
for income, expenses, assets and accounts payable during the year ended December 31,
2023. This was observed at eighteen (18) schools out of nineteen (19) visited in Harare,
Mashonaland West, Mashonaland Central, Masvingo and Matabeleland South. In the absence
of ledgers, I could not verify the correctness of income of ZWL$9 341 011 120, expenditure of
ZWL$7 215 348 362, assets of ZWL$3 825 844 337 and liabilities of ZWL$2 317 767 216 for
the eighteen (18) schools disclosed in the financial statements.

270

Risk/Implication
Without adequate accounting records, the financial statements may be misstated.
Recommendation
The Ministry should ensure that schools maintain ledgers and appropriate staff are appointed
and trained.
Management Response
The observation is noted. Some schools may not be maintaining ledgers due to financial
management matters being handled by unqualified personnel. Recognizing this, in 2022
the Ministry initiated a significant nationwide effort to address the gap by providing
Finance Management Training (FMT) to at least 5 000 schools. This comprehensive
financial management skills program included all government school headmasters and
selected local authority schools.

To further support this initiative, an updated FMT Manual was developed and distributed
to all schools across the country earlier in 2024, ensuring standardized and effective
financial management practices.

In addition, the Ministry is proactively working to resolve the issue of ledger
maintenance through the acquisition of an advanced accounting software package.
This software, planned for implementation in 2025, aims to enhance the efficiency and
accuracy of financial management across all our government schools.
(ii)     Completeness of Income Disclosed
Findings
Examination fees amounting to ZWL$142 054 913 collected by Amandas Primary school on
behalf of the Zimbabwe Schools Examination Council were incorrectly recognised as income.
Therefore, the income disclosed in the financial statements may be incorrect.
Further, Esigodini Primary School maintained two (2) different ZWL$ School Services Fund
(SSF) bank accounts. Revenue received through the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe (CBZ)
amounting to ZWL$2 588 378 was omitted in the financial statements. Also, Mushumbi High
School did not disclose in the financial statements the closing bank balance of US$3 569
(ZWL$21 787 746). As a result of the omission, I was not able to validate the completeness of
the income disclosed in the financial statements.
 Risk/Implication
Loss of accountability of revenue collected and misstatement of financial statements.

 Recommendations
Reconciliation between bank and financial statements should be carried out to ensure
accountability of all revenue collected.
Management should review and ensure that all receipts are included in the financial statements
in order to fully account for revenue.


271

Management Response

Amandas Primary School:  The observation is noted. Corrections will be made to
address the error.
Mushumbi High School: The observation is noted. The school will submit training needs
to the District Schools Inspector for consideration.
Esigodini Primary School: The school management will ensure that financial statements
are reviewed by a senior person.

Findings

Total expenditure recorded in the Appropriation Account amounted to ZWL$618 268 053 781

Furthermore, the Ministry’s Sub-Paymaster General’s Account Reconciliation Statement had

Bank statement revealed rejections of ZWL$255 748 909. I was not provided with an

The Ministry’s Sub-Paymaster General’s Account Reconciliation Statement had arithmetic

of ZWL$70 907 499.

not explained nor supported.

Risks/Implications

Fraud or errors may go undetected if the Statement of the Sub-Paymaster General’s Account
Reconciliation is not properly prepared and variances investigated.

297

Misstatement of financial statements.

Recommendations

Management should ensure that the variances are investigated and reconciliations done.

The errors noted should be investigated and cleared.

The variance of ZWL$107 873 003 829 between the Appropriation Account and the Sub-
Paymaster General’s Account emanated from unfunded transactions in the system that
are in the process of being reversed.

The observation in respect of the differences between the Treasury Releases according
to the Sub-Paymaster General Account Reconciliation Statement and the Treasury
Releases as per the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) is noted.

The cumulative amount of ZWL$410 488 992 included an amount of ZWL$154 799 948
which was a converted figure of direct deposits of US$30 253 that was made into the
Ministry’s NOSTRO account.

The errors in calculations are noted. There was a computational error on the excel
workbook which then led to the variances. We have however corrected the error.

There was wrong use of ‘Exchange Difference’ instead of ‘Reconciliation Difference’ as
it pertains to the difference between the Sub-PMG bank account and the PFMS balances.
Furthermore, the difference also significantly emanated from the computational error.
Thus, the actual difference after correcting the error is ZWL$6 056 665 and the issue is

The Ministry acquired goods and services amounting to ZWL$200 971 602 without obtaining

Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion

(i)
Disclosure Notes to Financial Statements

 Finding

The amounts disclosed in the notes to the consolidated financial statements were extracted
from the tertiary institutions’ individual statement of comprehensive income and statement of
financial position instead of taking from the notes to the financial statements of each tertiary
institution where more details are provided. The details that explain the basis behind reported
amounts were not reflected in the notes to the consolidated financial statements. This made it
difficult to validate the accuracy and completeness of the amounts in the consolidated financial
statements.

Risk/Implication

The consolidated financial statements may be misstated and hence not informative.

Recommendation

from the notes on individual tertiary institution financial statements.

(ii)   Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows

Findings

The 2021 consolidated statement of cash flows had many errors such that its relevance and
usefulness was lost. There were adjustments made to prior year account balances for
depreciation, suspense, assets, receivables and payables of ZWL$29 168, ZWL$1 020,
ZWL$19 320, ZWL$2 170 645 and ZWL$96 276 respectively. No details were provided on the
nature of the adjustments. The accuracy of cash and cash equivalents balances disclosed in
the consolidated statement of cash flows could not therefore, be confirmed in the absence of
details of the adjustments.

There was a variance of ZWL$1 237 005 594 between the cash and cash equivalents balance
of ZWL$1 575 660 837 as per the statement of cash flows and an amount of
ZWL$338 655 243 disclosed in the statement of financial position.

The consolidated statement of cash flows for 2020 had a variance of ZWL$5 639 282 between
cash and cash equivalents of ZWL$52 222 327 reflected in the statement of cash flows and
an amount of ZWL$46 583 045 disclosed in the statement of financial position. Furthermore,
an unexplained suspense figure of ZWL$1 698 057 was included as cash flow from operating
activities. There was no evidence that the staff responsible were capacitated to enable
preparation of accurate consolidated financial statements.

Risk/Implication

The financial statements were misstated.

Recommendation

The Ministry should train its staff in preparation of consolidated statements of cash flow and
resubmit corrected statements.

Management Response

The observation is noted. Management will submit a new set of Statement of Cash
Flows.

1
GOVERNANCE ISSUES

1.1    Budget Utilisation

Finding

The total budget for the Ministry was ZWG 416 666 482 while funding provided amounted to
ZWG 257 929 697 resulting in a budget utilization of 62% of the voted funds. However, the
Ministry had arrear payments of ZWG 24 463 724 that could not be settled. Treasury was not
able to provide adequate funding to support the payments and other budgeted/planned
programs of the Ministry.

Risk/Implication

The Ministry may fail to achieve its objectives due to inadequate funding.

Recommendation

The Ministry should continue lobbying for funding from the Ministry of Finance, Economic
Development and Investment Promotion.


337

Management Response

Management did not respond.
1.2
Risk Management Policy and Annual Assessments

Finding

As highlighted in my previous report, the Ministry did not carry out risk assessments as well as
provide the risk profile report for audit. This was attributed to the absence of an approved risk
management policy document. Provisions of Section162 (1) and (3) of the Public Finance
Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 require Accounting Officers to carry out risk
assessment and also to submit a copy of the risk profile report to the Auditor-General annually.

Risk/Implication

The lack of a formal risk assessment process and approved policy document exposes the
Ministry to potential financial losses and reputational damage.

Recommendation

The Ministry should develop and approve a risk management policy document that provides
clear guidance on conducting risk assessments. This will enable the Ministry to proactively
identify and mitigate risks, ensuring better financial management and accountability.

Management Response

A draft Risk Management Policy was drafted in 2024 and submitted to the Ministry of
Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion for validation and
approval.

A workshop for risk champions was affected by lack of resources but once trained, the
Ministry would be able to prepare an enterprise risk register which is a critical tool when
assessing risk.

1.3
Audit Committee

Finding

The Audit Committee consisted of three (3) executive members, two (2) of whom were directly
responsible for implementing programs which compromised its independence and
effectiveness. This arrangement created a self-review threat, contravening good corporate
governance principles. Furthermore, the Committee did not meet during the financial year
ended December 31, 2024, to review internal controls and address control environment issues,
violating Section 84(3)(b) of the Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19], which
requires at least two meetings per year.

Risk/Implication

The Audit Committee's ineffectiveness may lead to inadequate oversight, allowing internal
control weaknesses and governance issues to go unaddressed.

Recommendations

The Ministry should appoint members who are not directly involved with Internal Audit function.
338

The Audit Committee should adhere to the requirements of the Public Finance Management
Act [Chapter 22:19], so that there is regular monitoring and evaluation of internal controls, risks
and compliance as well as governance issues.

Management Response

The observation was noted and the Ministry will appoint a majority of non-executive
members to the Audit Committee. The appointments will be guided by the recent cabinet
approved guidelines on the appointment of members to the Audit Committee.

1.4
Payment Arrears

Finding

Payment arrears increased by 89% from ZWG 2 750 051 in the prior year to ZWG 24 463 724
in the current year, with no evidence of timely settlement, potentially incurring unnecessary
penalties.

Risks/Implications

The accumulation of arrears if left unattended, erodes the budget of the subsequent year and
negatively impacts on service delivery and reputation.
The Ministry may be sued or penalized for late payments.
Recommendation

Management should prioritise payments to critical and long outstanding suppliers so as to
avoid disrupting essential services.

Management Response

The sharp increase in Payment Arrears in 2024 was as a result of failure by the
Accountant General Department to provide actual cash support for already committed
expenditure. The funding had been released in the system, resulting in the processing
of payment documents by the Ministry which were later reversed due to the
unavailability of actual cash support.

To solve the problem, in 2025 the Ministry prioritised the clearance of 2024 arrears in
compliance with Treasury Circular No 2 of 2025. The Ministry, in the first two budget
committee meetings committed to clear the 2024 debts by mid-2025.

Finding

I have audited the financial statements of the Ministry of Justice, Legal and Parliamentary

Qualified Opinion
In my opinion, except for the possible effects of the matters described in the Basis for Qualified

the state of affairs of the Ministry of Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs as at December

Basis for Qualified Opinion
(i)
Understatement of Appropriation Account Expenditure

Findings

The Master of High Court collected revenue amounting to ZWG44 273 713 and US$5 580 567
in respect of deceased estates fees and utilised ZWG24 807 493 and US$665 007 without
Parliamentary approval. The money was spent outside the PFM system and was not disclosed
in the Appropriation Account. This was caused by absence of regulations and guidelines on
the collection and use of the collected fees as required by Section 132 (2) (c) of the
Administration of Estates Act [Chapter 6:01]. I raised the same issue in my prior year audit
report.

Risks/Implications

Retention and use of funds without Parliamentary authority may result in unauthorised
expenditure.
359


The Appropriation Account was misstated due to non-inclusion of the expenditure.

Recommendations

The Master of the High Court should follow laid down procedures in accounting and utilising
public funds to avoid violating budgetary processes.

The Ministry should ensure that regulations and guidelines relating to accounting and reporting
for the retained monies are put in place in line with the Public Finance Management Act
[Chapter 22:19] and the Administration of Estates Act [Chapter 6:01].

In the absence of regulations on fees collected as required by the Administration of Estates
Act [Chapter 6:01, the Master of the High Court should surrender the revenue collected from
deceased estates to the Consolidated Revenue Fund in compliance with section 16 (2) of the
Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19].

Management Response

This has since been regularized by the enactment of the Administration of Estates
Amendment Act in November 2024 which established a Statutory Fund under section
4F.

Evaluation of Management Response

The expenditure incurred before the enactment of the Administration of Estates Amendment
Act in November 2024 outside the Public Financial Management System was not disclosed in
the Appropriation Account.

(ii)    Misstatement of Compensation of Employees
Finding

Compensation of employees’ expenditure amounting to ZWL$175 164 106 929 for the period
January to April 2024 was converted to ZWG70 101 417 using incorrect rate of 2498.7242
instead of the spot rate. However, if spot rates as guided by Treasury were used the result
would have been ZWG132 947 495. Therefore, there was a variance of ZWG62 846 078
resulting in the misstatement of compensation of employees.

Risk/ Implication
The Compensation of employee’s expenditure in the Appropriation Account was misstated.

Recommendation

The Ministry should use conversion rates prescribed in Treasury Circular Number 1 of 2025 to
avoid misstatement of account balances.

Management Response

The observation is noted, the Ministry used the rate of 2498.7242 to convert
compensation of employees’ cost because salaries were paid directly to SSB by
Treasury. The Ministry did not have access to the bank statement for us to know the
transaction dates for compensation of employees’ expenditure.


360

(iii)  Receipts and Disbursements

 Findings

The Statement of Receipts and Disbursements submitted for audit had an opening balance of
ZWG10 085 937, collections of ZWG672 768 400, total payments and adjustments to the
Exchequer and other accounts of ZWG678 183 538 and these amounts should have given a
closing balance of ZWG4 670 800. However, the closing balance disclosed on the Statement
was ZWG305 485 671 resulting in an unexplained variance of ZWG300 814 871. Therefore, I
could not place reliance on the closing balance disclosed on the Statement of Receipts and
Disbursements.

Furthermore, the return had an incorrect opening balance of ZWG10 085 937 instead of the
prior year closing balance of ZWG328 097 resulting in a variance of ZWG9 757 840. There
were no explanations provided for the adjustments.

The Statement of receipts and disbursements submitted for audit disclosed transfers to the
Exchequer amounting to ZWG496 189 680 whereas the underlying records in the PFMS had
transfers amounting to ZWG29 258 579 resulting in an unreconciled variance of
ZWG466 931 101.

Risk/Implication

Misstatement of Receipts and Disbursements.

Recommendation

The Ministry should correct the Statement of Receipts and Disbursements return and reconcile
the variances noted.

Management Response

The variance of ZWG300 814 871 was caused by the use of the multi-currency which is
now affecting the presentation of receipts and disbursement template resulting in no
link between the opening balance and other columns. The variance of ZWG466 931 101
was caused by transfer of funds which are still work in progress.

Legal Aid Directorate and the Courts Fund held by the Attorney General`s Office retain
funds. Imbalances are emanating from different exchange rates.

Evaluation of Management Response

Findings on transfers to other accounts and imbalances on the Statement were not addressed
as the variances were not reconciled.

(iv) Sub-Paymaster General Account Reconciliations

Finding
The Appropriation Account had total expenditure amounting to ZWG1 993 080 865
whereas the Sub-Paymaster General’s Account (Sub-PMG) disclosed expenditure amounting
to ZWG1 954 277 094, resulting in a variance of ZWG38 803 771 that was not reconciled. The
Appropriation Account expenditure was converted to ZWG using spot rates while the
expenditure in Sub-PMG reconciliation was converted using a rate of 2 498.7242. This
contributed to the variance of ZWG38 803 771.
361

Risk/Implication

Failure to use prescribed rates in the preparation of the Appropriation Account and the Sub-
PMG resulted in misstatement of the account balances disclosed.

Recommendation

The Ministry should use conversion rates prescribed in Treasury Circular Number 1 of 2025 to
avoid misstatement of account balances.

Management Response
We used the Reserve Bank and SSB rate of 2498.7242 to convert all transactions in
disclosed in Sub PMG from ZWL to ZWG instead of the spot rates because it enabled
us to reconcile the Ministry’s Sub PMG balance and the closing bank balance without
leaving a variance.

(v)
Annual Closure Certificate

 Finding

The Annual Closure Certificate showed that the Ministry had open and un-cleared transactions
in the Receipting Cashbook General Ledger amounting to ZWG503 126 092. Treasury Circular
Number 1 of 2025, requires all open items in the system to be cleared before preparation of
bank reconciliations, annual returns and financial statements to ensure completeness and
alignment. I could not therefore, validate with certainty the accuracy and completeness of the
revenue received reported amounting to ZWG738 022 337.

Risk/Implication

The revenue received reported in the Statement of Revenue Received could be misstated.

Recommendation

Management should clear all outstanding open transactions in general ledgers to ensure
completeness and alignment of financial statements.

Management Response
Treasury delayed configuration of the Sales and Distribution Module in the SAP system
as it was configured on the 31st of December 2024. The Ministry then organized for a
training workshop for its members to train on the module which then inputted all 2024
revenues into the system. The clearing of open items is still work in progress.

GOVERNANCE ISSUES

1.1
Risk Management Policy

Finding

The Fund did not have a risk management policy to assist management in mitigating potential
risks that may hamper its operation. No risk assessments were carried out during the year
under review. Section 162(1) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019
requires Accounting Officers to carry out risk assessment of their operations on an annual
basis and take deliberate steps to identify, quantify, assess and come up with mitigation
measures for the risks identified.



372

Risk/Implication

Without a risk management policy, the Fund is susceptible to numerous risks like fraud which
could negatively impact on its performance.

Recommendations

The Accounting officer should expedite the development and approval of a risk management
policy to guide in mitigating risks associated with the nature of its operations.

Risk assessments should be carried out regularly and timeously in order to identify and take
preventative measures on potential risks.

Management Response

The observation is noted. The Fund has an Investment Committee which is responsible
for risk assessment. The Fund is in transition and this has affected developing and
implementing strategy as this should be informed by the changes in the new Act. As
soon as the entity is established as an autonomous Office, strategy formulation and all
policy issues will be addressed including the Guardian’s Fund risk policy.

Evaluation of Management Response

Terms of reference of the Investment Committee did not cover assessment of the overall risks
that may hamper the Fund and there was no evidence of risk assessment carried out during
the year under review.

Investment Strategy

Finding

and ZWL$2 617 124 687 respectively without investment advisors’ recommendations. Section

investment advisors to help the Master in investment matters. Therefore, I could not establish
whether the investments made during the year under review were the most economic ones.

Risk/Implication

Making investments without requisite investment recommendations may result in uneconomic
returns on investments.

Recommendation

Administrators of the Fund should make use of investment advisors to avoid loss of funds due
to uneconomic investment decisions.

management has established an Investment Committee approved by the Secretary.

1        GOVERNANCE ISSUES

1.1
Statement of Payment Arrears

As at December 31, 2024, the Ministry had arrear payments due to various suppliers and
service providers totaling ZWG3 460 687, with some invoices dating back to May 2024. As at
April 8, 2025, the arrear payments had been reduced to ZWG1 125 366. There was no
evidence that these liabilities were periodically reported to Treasury for funding to facilitate
clearance.

Risk/Implication
Arrear payments have the effect of consuming the current budget thereby affecting operations
of the Ministry.
Recommendation
The Ministry should continuously engage Treasury so that the outstanding balances are
settled.

The Ministry reversed all documents processed in the year 2024, which did not receive
cash support from Treasury. The arrears accumulated due to delayed payments for
goods and services that had already been supplied to the Ministry. The Ministry is
451

actively engaging Treasury to ensure that arrear payments are avoided in the future as
they affect current operations.
1.2    Open Items

Finding

The Ministry had open items amounting to ZWG24 912 110 in the Public Finance Management
System (Cash Book) that were not cleared. The open items comprised of salaries that were
paid directly on behalf of the Ministry. This amount was included as expenditure in the
Ministry's Appropriation Account and awaits Treasury to clear the amounts.

Risk/Implication

Unresolved open items can create uncertainties in cashflow management.

Recommendation

The Ministry should engage Treasury and clear all open items in the system.

Management Response
The open items are in respect of direct payments made by Treasury on behalf of the
Ministry. The clearance of these items requires an input from Treasury, which is
necessary for the Ministry to complete the process. The Ministry remains committed to
comply with the requirements of Treasury Circular Number 1 of 2025 and will engage
with Treasury to ensure the timely resolution of these open items.
1.3
Budget Utilisation
 Finding

An analysis of the Ministry’s total budget, budget releases, and funding provided by the
Treasury revealed that out of the total budget of ZWG142 972 660, operations and capital
expenditure funded ZWG48 693 330 representing 34% while compensation of employees was
fully funded at ZWG6 884 708 representing 5% giving a budget utilisation of 39%. The budget
underutilisation was mainly due to non-release of funding by Treasury as a result of lack of
liquidity. However, due to this non release of funding the Ministry at year end owed ZWG3 460
687 to service providers and suppliers.

Risk/Implication

Inadequate funding compromised the Ministry's ability to deliver its mandate effectively.

Recommendation
The Ministry should continually engage Treasury to provide funding for its operations.
Management Response

Treasury did not release budget as guided by the cash flows that the Ministry submitted
at the beginning of the year. The budget releases were increased towards the end of the
year but these were not followed by cash support. This led to reversals amounting to
ZWG22 541 081.90. This non funding by Treasury impacted negatively on the Ministry’s
452

operations and the relationship with its suppliers. The suppliers are now reluctant to
provide goods and services upfront as they are owed ZWG3 460 687.
The Ministry has paid almost half of the arrears using the 2025 budget. Arrears are
therefore affecting operations for 2025. The Ministry will continue to engage Treasury
to secure adequate funding for the Ministry’s operations.

Finding

discretion to determine the other grades/levels that can be allocated fuel. However, I noted
that a blanket allocation of fuel which was said to be for operations was being issued to every
member in the Ministry. Fuel for operations cannot be given as a blanket issue but on a need
basis in the course of carrying out Government business.

Risks/Implications

Inefficient usage of fuel.

Misappropriation of fuel.

Recommendation

The Accounting Officer should revisit the approved allocations to correct the anomaly of
blanket allocation of operations fuel to every member. Operations fuel should be allocated
whenever need arises.

When the Ministry was established, it did not have any tools of trade including vehicles
and therefore Officers were allocated fuel to enable them to perform their duties. The
Ministry will implement the recommendations of the Auditor-General as the situation

 1.5   Travel and Subsistence Ledger Cards and Register

Finding

The Ministry incurred ZWG5 986 156 in Traveling and Subsistence expenses during the 2024
financial year. However, my review of Travel and Subsistence records revealed that the ledger
cards and registers were not updated. This affects the Ministry's ability to effectively track
amounts advanced to officers for travel, settlements and follow up on outstanding advances.
Section 64 (5) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 requires that
efficient controls and accounting records be maintained in respect of all advances made.

 Risk/Implication

 Without updated records it becomes difficulty in tracking and recovering outstanding advances.

Recommendation

The Ministry should ensure that travel and subsistence ledger cards and register are updated.
453

Management Response

The Ministry was maintaining a travel and subsistence register since there were no cash
advances. The recommendation is noted and the Ministry is updating the ledgers and

1.6    Risk Management and Assessment

 Finding

The Ministry had a draft risk management policy in place and no formal risk assessments were
carried out to cover key business processes in the year under review. The Ministry used its

Failure to carry out formal risk assessments may expose the Ministry to numerous risks which

Recommendation

The Ministry should perform and document risk assessments on an annual basis to safeguard
Government funds and assets.

Management Response

The Ministry has a draft Risk assessment policy. The draft is still being validated at the
same time when Ministry departments are being established and furthermore
engagements with new staff remains work in progress. The internal Audit department

Ministry.

2      MANAGEMENT OF ASSETS

Finding

The Ministry did not capture assets in the Public Finance Management System (PFMS). During

454

Management should ensure that all assets are captured in the PFM system in compliance

The assets need to be uploaded on the PFMS system using excel worksheets. The

Below are issues noted during the audit:

1.
GOVERNANCE ISSUES
1.1
Witness Expenses
Finding
From a sample of thirteen (13) courts visited, it was noted that witnesses were only reimbursed
transport allowances even though they qualified for other allowances which included detention
and meals. This was contrary to the Accounting Officer’s Instructions which require that they
be paid other allowances. These allowances were meant to encourage them to attend court
sessions willingly without over-burdening them with costs, to facilitate justice delivery.
However, audit noted that some witnesses, for example at Headlands, had to sleep at bus
terminuses so as to attend the weekly circuit court.

Risk/Implication
This could negatively affect service delivery as witnesses may fail to present themselves in
459

courts due to economic hardships thereby affecting case clearance rate and justice delivery.

Recommendation

Witnesses should be reimbursed all the expenses including detention and meals they incur
when they attend court sessions. The Commission should consider other reimbursement
methods such as mobile money transfer facilities.

Management Response

Management acknowledges that witnesses have been reimbursed transport allowances
only, despite their eligibility for additional allowances, including detention and meals.
Management recognizes the importance of ensuring that witnesses are adequately
compensated for their expenses, particularly given the challenging economic
environment. The limitation on providing full reimbursement can be attributed to several
factors including Zimbabwe’s Banking Restrictions.

The on-going shortage of local currency has made it difficult to provide adequate cash
allowances. This has resulted in prioritizing transport reimbursements as they are
deemed essential for witnesses to attend court sessions.

Existing policies regarding witness allowances may not have been updated to reflect
the current economic realities. This has inadvertently led to the under-compensation of
witnesses for necessary expenses incurred while attending court.

The Commission did not indicate the steps they are taking to address the anomaly of under-
reimbursements to witnesses.

accounting package. Section 119 (1) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury
Instructions), 2019, requires transactions to be accounted for through the PFMS unless the
Accountant-General has authorized the use of an independent package. There was no
authority produced for use of the PASTEL package.

Risk/Implication

Unapproved accounting packages may lack integration capabilities causing compatibility
issues and decreased efficiency.

Recommendation

Management should comply with the requirements of Treasury Instructions or obtain authority
for use of the PASTEL system.

The observation is noted. The transactions of the Fund have been recorded using the
PASTEL accounting package, which according to the said regulations, should only be
460

used if authorized by the Accountant-General.

The Commission remains committed to complying with all Treasury requirements and
will take necessary steps to ensure that the Fund’s accounting practices align with
statutory regulations.

Finding

The Commission submitted the 2022 Financial Statements for audit on February 16, 2024.

Basis for Qualified Opinion

(i)
Open Items

 Finding

The Commission did not clear open items in the PFMS revenue and expenditure ledgers. Open
items with a value of ZWG13 443 064 that remained uncleared represent revenue collected
but not yet receipted in the system. Expenditure items with a value of ZWG8 721 237 343 also
remained uncleared in the PFMS. Treasury Circular No. 1 of 2025 requires Accounting Officers
to clear all open items in the system before preparation of annual returns and financial
statements to ensure completeness. I could not therefore, place reliance on the revenue and
expenditure reported in the financial statements.

Risk/Implication

Revenue and expenditure may not be accurately recognised.




464

Recommendation

Management should ensure that all uncleared items on the Revenue and Expenditure SAP
ledgers are cleared.

Management Response

The observation is acknowledged. The increase in uncleared open items was primarily
due to technical challenges within the SAP system which delayed reconciliations and
clearing processes. The transition from client 500 to client 600 introduced system
challenges. On January 09, 2025, the Public Service Commission wrote to the Ministry
of Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion requesting assistance
to resolve these issues.

The Commission is actively working with the Ministry of Finance, Economic
Development and Investment Promotion and SAP support teams to address the
problems and clear all outstanding items. Management remains committed to fully
complying with Treasury Circular No. 1 of 2025 and enhancing the accuracy of financial
reporting.

Audit Committee

Finding
The Audit Committee comprised of four (4) members who were employees of the Commission

Finding

The Commission had an approved budget of ZWG2 377 691 564 and the funding that was

 The Budget underutilization was mainly due to non-release of funding by Treasury as a

Finding

If the payment arrears are not monitored and reported, they will continue accumulating

Regular engagements should be done with the Ministry of Finance and Economic

2
REVENUE COLLECTION AND DEBT RECOVERY
2.1    Recovery of Debts
 Finding
 As previously reported, the Commission has not been effective in the management of debt.
During the year under review Outstanding Revenue increased by more than 100% from
ZWG520 719 in 2023 to ZWG37 308 907. Outstanding Surcharges increased by over 100%
from ZWG852 510 in 2023 to ZWG3 006 198 and Outstanding Disallowances increased by
6.55% from ZWG2 432 495 in 2023 to ZWG2 591 823. Section 49(2) of the Public Finance
Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 requires Officers responsible for collecting debts to
take adequate steps to collect any sums due to the Government on the due date.
Risk/Implication
The absence of effective strategies, to recover debts may result in loss of funds due to lapse
of time.
Recommendation
The Ministry should ensure that the outstanding debts are regularly monitored and robust
mechanisms are put in place to ensure quick recovery.
Management Response
Management acknowledges the observation. The Commission has developed various
strategies to manage and recover the debts. These include the following:

• A working relationship with banks in which funds paid to pensioners are recalled
in cases where the funds have not been utilised.

• A working relationship with the Registrar General (RG)’s Office in which deceased
Pensioners are detected and removed from the Pension payroll.

• Resuscitation of the dormant account facility in which banks periodically flag
individual accounts for Pensioners which are inactive.

• Pension awareness campaigns are periodically carried out to raise awareness of
Government pension procedures and steps that should be taken in the event of
the death of a pensioner,

• Rolling out biometric system to provinces and districts and completion of life
certificates and

• Engagement of Chiefs throughout the country to help in identifying deaths of
pensioners.

Revenue Receipted Outside the System

Finding

The Commission manually receipted revenue from Bus fares and commission from the

467

Instructions), 2019 states that the preferred method of acknowledging receipt of funds is
through electronic receipts.

Risk/ Implication

Manually receipting revenue may result failure to fully account for all revenue collected.

Recommendation

The Public Service Commission should ensure that all the revenue received is processed
through the PFMS system.

Management Response

Management acknowledges the observation. Following a change of currency from ZWL
to ZWG in April 2024, there was a long period of system down time as Treasury was
creating new client 600. This affected receipting in the system up to the year end of
2024, however the SAP system is now up and running and all receipts done outside the
system are being introduced into the system.

Approval of Rates or Tariffs

Finding

The Commission did not submit approved revenue rates or tariffs for the fees it charges for its
services under the various revenue heads. As a result, I was not able to ascertain the

Risks/ Implications

Absence of a clear, approved fee structure, may result in inconsistent application of charges
for services offered.

Revenue may be lost due to use of incorrect tariffs/rates.

Recommendation

The Commission should avail the approved rates for audit.

The observation is noted. The Commission will in future seek Treasury approval before

1.2  Disbursements of Loans
 Findings

During the year under review, the Fund disbursed loans amounting to ZWL$534 804 619
against loan applications of ZWL$665 485 096. However, the Fund invested
ZWL$2 080 778 366 which was a significant amount as compared to loan applications and
loans approved and disbursed. Paragraph 4 of the Fund’s Constitution states that the objective
of the Fund is to provide financial assistance to members in the form of loans or similar
instruments.

A substantial amount of the member contributions went towards investments. Audit analysis
of the loan application process revealed that it takes from six (6) months to more than one (1)
year, for one to access the funds, potentially discouraging members.

Risk/Implication

Having large sums of funds invested does not further the mandate of the Fund which is to
provide financial assistance to members in the form of loans or similar instruments.

474

Recommendations
The Fund should bring awareness to contributing members for them to apply for the loans.

The Fund should simplify the application process and reduce processing time so that
members benefit from the Fund.

Management Response

For the period under consideration, total employee Treasury contributions and loan
repayments received amounted to ZWL$4 506 275 913 against loan demands of
ZWL$665 485 096. Therefore, it was prudent for the Fund to invest excess funds which
is in line with the Fund’s Constitution. Furthermore, the Commission had directed that
excess funds be invested in order to grow the Fund thereby generating wealth that
benefits members upon retirement.

Evaluation of Management Response

The management response is acknowledged. However, the response did not address the
finding on why the Fund invested money instead of issuing loans to its subscribing members
so that they benefit as they contribute rather than upon retirement given that this is a Mutual
and not a Pension Fund.

1.3    Investments Management Agreement

Finding

Management did not avail for examination investment management agreements between
GEMS Fund with its asset managers. Section 53 (16) of the Public Finance Management
(Treasury Instructions), 2019 requires Accounting Officers to ensure that all contracts are in
writing and expressed in appropriate terms.

Risk/ Implication

It will be difficult to monitor or enforce performance in the absence of valid investment
management agreements.

Recommendation

The Fund should have documented contracts with its asset managers to enhance monitoring
and enforcement of performance.

Management Response

The GEMS Fund and the Pension Management Fund utilises the same institutional
infrastructure. As a result, GEMS Fund utilized the existing Service Level Agreement
(SLA) of Pension Management Fund that had already been signed. Thus, GEMS Fund
leveraged on the establishment agreement to avoid the time and costs associated with
creating a new SLA. Leveraging on the established SLA not only conserved resources
but also provided a solid foundation for ongoing operations, enhancing the overall
efficiency and effectiveness of the Fund’s management activities.



475

Evaluation of Management Response

Management response is noted. However, the Fund needs to have its name added to the
existing Service Level Agreements that are relied upon.

The Fund had a net defined benefit liability position of ZWL$3 214 069 818 266 as at December
31, 2022 as indicated on Note 11. In addition, pension receivables increased by 1 424% from
ZWL$753 817 044 in 2021 to ZWL$11 491 846 807 in 2022. There were no mechanisms in
place to recover the amounts. The continual increase in pension receivables will result in loss
of revenue as they become irrecoverable due to lapse of time. These conditions indicate the
existence of material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt about the Fund’s ability to
continue operating as a going concern. However, my opinion is not modified in respect of this
matter.

GOVERNANCE ISSUES
1.1  Supporting Documents for Investments

Finding

The Fund paid ZWL$2 227 340 377 for the purchase of fourteen (14) shares in Kuvimba Mining
House (Private) Limited through Chimukamafunga. While a dividend of ZWL$58,9 million was
received, there were no supporting documents such as share certificates to confirm the nature,
value and ownership of the investment.

481

Risk/Implication
The value of shares could be misstated in the financial statements.
Recommendation
The Fund should ensure that the nominal value of the shares is recorded on the face of the
share certificate.
Management Response
In accordance with the Act, the share certificate clearly indicate that the shares have no
nominal or par value denomination. This aligns with the transitional provisions outlined
in Section 304, which state that “share certificates issued for shares without par value
do not need to display the par value.”
Evaluation of Management Response

Management response is noted. The share certificate without the nominal or par value was not
submitted for audit.
1.2  Actuarial Liabilities

Findings
The financial statements showed an actuarial valuation of liabilities of ZWL$3,3 trillion while
net plan assets were ZWL$98.2 billion resulting in a shortfall of ZWL$3,2 trillion. The Fund's
liabilities outweigh its assets by a significant margin, this places the Fund's ability to meet its
future pension obligations at risk.
Contributions made to date from the Ministry of Finance, Economic Development and
Investment Promotion of ZWL$70.4 million after the formation of the Fund, do not match the
retirement benefits to be covered.
Risk/Implication
The Fund will fail to meet the retirement benefit liability obligations.
Recommendation
The Fund should engage Treasury to have more capital injection to cover the gap between
actuarial liabilities and the plan assets.
Management Response
The audit observation is noted. Treasury acknowledged that a fully funded pension plan
will take the place of the Pay as you go in line with Section 142 of the 2021 National
Budget Statement and this fully funded pension plan requires an equivalent of US$4.8
billion to cover the pension liability according to 2012 actuarial valuation report. The
Government’s goal is to gradually enable the Fund achieve its objective of advancing
and safeguarding pension contributions and pensioners’ rights.
Accordingly, Treasury pledged to finance the Fund to cover both the Actuarial Liabilities
and capital injections to cater for members who had contributed prior to the
establishment of the Fund by bringing in other assets. Treasury indicated that it is in
482

the process of identifying assets to be ceded to the Fund.

Internal Audit Reports
Finding

during the year under review. Section 161 (1) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury
Instructions), 2019, requires the Accounting Officer to ensure that internal audits are carried
out.
Risk/ Implication
A weak internal control environment may prevail that will lead to fraud and errors.
Recommendation
The Fund management should ensure that an Internal Audit reviews the Fund’s internal
controls during the year.

The observation is noted.  For the year under review, the internal audit was unable to
carry out the audit of the Pension Management Fund Account due to the fact that the

Finding

The lease agreement requires rentals to be paid in advance on or before the first day of each

According to the lease agreements, rental income will be collected in advance and

1.2  Fuel Management

Findings

During the period September 07, 2023 extending to October 31, 2024, the Commission lost
21 800 litres of diesel and 3 400 litres of petrol valued at ZWG650 122 through fraudulent
activities attributed to a number of control weaknesses within the fuel management system.
This was according to the special investigation report issued by the Central Internal Audit Unit
dated March 19, 2025.

The loss was attributed to lack of segregation of duties as the administration officer responsible
for fuel had sole access of custody to the safe key as well as the spare keys. Supervisory
checks on the work of the Administration officer were found to be lacking as fuel was being
issued haphazardly without following serial number sequences. Fuel coupons’ serial numbers
were sometimes skipped and duplicated. Records were altered in the fuel register through
pasting. Vehicle log books were not being reconciled to the fuel issued. Section 104(1) of the
Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019.

Risk/Implication

Program objectives and service delivery may be compromised if fuel is misappropriated.

Recommendation

The Commission’s management should strengthen controls around fuel management in order
to safeguard state resources. Those found responsible for the misappropriation should be
asked to make good the loss.

Management Response

Internal controls around fuel management have been enhanced and are now in place to
help detect and prevent fraudulent activities in the fuel management. The Commission
has strengthened its internal control systems through segregation of duties in the
administration of fuel. The Director Finance and Administration is now responsible for
writing letters to Petrotrade for the collections of fuel and the Deputy Director
Administration is now responsible for the collection of fuel coupons.

Documents for bulk fuel collected are now handed over to Director Finance and
Administration for recording. The Director Finance and Administration retains the
coupons for safe keeping if it is not for immediate issuance and hands over to the
Administration officer fuel for current operations. Periodic Supervisory checks are
being done and enhanced filing of all fuel requisitions, receipts and logbooks is now in
place.

The Finance Team disintegrates the two (2) on a separate sheet that is attached to the
payment vouchers. The amounts in the PFMS and the actual wage bills that Finance
uses differ because of timing exchange rates. The wage bills are sent to MDAs around
the 10th of each month, yet Treasury makes direct payment to SSB on or around the 25th
of same month. Resultantly there are timing differences as the exchange rate fluctuates
between the two dates. The Commission has engaged Treasury to assist in clearing the
amounts.

Commission management should reconcile the variance due to exchange rate differences to
account for the compensation of employees disclosed.

1.1
Budget Utilisation
Findings

The Commission received from Treasury funding amounting to ZWG80 431 393 which
constituted 89% of the total budget. Funding that went towards operations and capital
expenditure was 73% of the budget while 16% went towards compensation of employees.
However, at year end the Commission had outstanding payment arrears of ZWG5 934 722
due to suppliers. There was no evidence that the payments had been settled at the time of
concluding my audit on April 28, 2025.

I further noted that, part of the outstanding payments amounting to ZWG445 183 (16% of the
total ZWG payment arrears) were for domestic travel expenses and US$25 149 (20% of the
total US$ payment arrears) for foreign travel expenses owed to staff members. The payments
date back as far as January 2024 and remained outstanding at the time of concluding my audit
on April 28, 2025.

Risks/Implications

The arrears if not paid, impacts on the budget of the subsequent year.

2
MANAGEMENT OF ASSETS

2.1    Motor Vehicles
Finding
The Commission received from the Ministry of Finance four (4) vehicles that were forfeited to
the State by Zimbabwe Revenue Authority between April 2019 and July 2021. The vehicles
have not been registered for more than 5 years. Section 103 (4) of Public Finance Management
(Treasury Instructions), 2019, requires Accounting Officers to ensure that all Ministry/
Commission vehicles (including donated vehicles) have been registered under the Ministry/
Commission.
Risk/Implication
Ownership of the vehicles can be questionable if they remain in the original owner’s name and
this can create administrative complications.
Recommendation
The Commission should comply with the regulation by ensuring that the vehicles are properly
registered.
Management Response
The Commission is now working on registering the vehicles after Treasury disbursed
funds for their registration in March 2025.
2.2  Donations
Findings
The Commission received donations worth US$2 298 without Treasury authority contrary to
Section 112 (1) of the Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 which states
that Treasury shall direct whether gifts or donations shall be accepted or not. Treasury
Authority was only sought on February 24, 2025 when donations had been received in 2024.
Furthermore, the donations were not recorded in the temporary assets register pending
Treasury Authority.
Risks/Implications
Unauthorised donations which have a charge against the Consolidated Revenue Fund may
be received by the Commission.
518

Assets received may be exposed to theft and misappropriation if not recorded.
Recommendation
The Commission should obtain Treasury Authority for all donations received before they are
put into use.
Management Response
The Commission sought Treasury Concurrence for the items and will make a follow up
with Treasury for authority.

I have audited the Appropriation Account of the Zimbabwe Land Commission for the year
ended December 31, 2024 and I issued an unmodified opinion.

Opinion

In my opinion, the financial statements present fairly in all material respects, the state of affairs
of the Zimbabwe Land Commission for the year ended December 31, 2024 in accordance with
the Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19] and other relevant Statutory Instruments.

Below are issues noted during the audit:

1
GOVERNANCE ISSUES

1.1
Budget Utilization

 Finding

 The total budget allocation for the Commission was ZWG85 367 909 while funding provided
amounted to ZWG58 517 727 for operations resulting in a budget utilisation of 69% of the
voted funds. However, the Commission had arrear payments of ZWG36 237 577 that could
not be settled. Treasury was not able to provide adequate funding to support the payments
and other budgeted/ planned programs of the Commission.


Risk/Implication

Not releasing funding as per budgeted amounts might negatively affect service delivery.

Recommendation

Management should liaise with Treasury to ensure that total budgeted funds are released
timeously to meet the expenditure of the Commission.

Management Response

The observation is noted. The Commission will continue to liaise with Treasury on
funding of committed expenditures in the current year so as to avoid carrying over of
520

debts to the next financial year. However, with the introduction and migration to accrual
basis, such issues will be systematically solved.

1.2
Disaster Recovery/ Business Continuity Plan

 Finding

The Commission had no Disaster Recovery Plan to enable it to continue offering critical
services in the event of a system disruption and to survive a disastrous interruption of services.
Section 44 (1) (a) (i) of the Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19], requires an
Accounting Authority for a public entity to establish and maintain an effective and transparent
system of financial and risk management and internal control.

 Risk/Implication

 Data can be lost without recovery in the event of an unforeseen tragedy.

Recommendation

The Commission should come up with a Disaster Recovery Plan to enable continuity of
services in the event of a disaster.

Management Response

The observation is noted. A Risk Management and Disaster Recovery Plan workshop
was conducted in October 2024 to produce Risk Registers and Disaster Recovery Plan.
However, the Disaster Recovery Plan output could not be completed within the training
programme resulting in postponement of production of the Disaster Recovery Plan to
2025. In this regard, the Disaster Recovery Plan would be produced by December 31,
2025.

2      MANAGEMENT OF ASSETS
2.1
Maintenance of Asset Register
Finding

The Commission did not upload assets on the Public Financial Management System (PFMS)
asset register during the year under review in contravention of Section 100 (1) and (5) of the
Public Finance Management (Treasury Instructions), 2019 which requires the director
responsible for administration to ensure that the manual asset registers are reconciled
regularly with the respective ministry’s asset control account maintained on the PFMS. This
was caused by lack of training of the administration personnel on how to capture the assets.

Risk/Implication

The existence, ownership and accountability of state property may be compromised.

Recommendation

The Commission should train personnel in the use of PFMS so that assets are uploaded on
the System.


521

Management Response

In the year 2024, the Commission reached out to the Ministry of Finance, Economic
Development, and Investment Promotion, requesting the training on the SAP Asset
Management Module. The Projects Office verbally conveyed that it was not ready to
conduct training for the SAP Asset Management Module, citing ongoing alignment with
IPSAS requirements. In 2025, the Commission intends to follow up with the Treasury
regarding the availability of training for the SAP Asset Management Module. This
initiative aims to implement the audit recommendations, as stipulated in the Treasury
Instructions.

report as outlined below.

was done in the 2nd quarter of 2024.
3.2    Disaster Recovery/ Business Continuity Plan

The Commission was working on Disaster Recovery /Business Continuity Plan. Workshop was
conducted in October 2024 with a Consultant facilitating the workshop but there was no
Disaster Recovery Plan that was drafted.

3.3    Land Disputes and Complaints Resolution

The issue of land disputes was resolved.

3.4
Institutional Gender Policy

The Gender Policy was still work in progress. It was a chapter in the Human Resources Policy.

3.5  Gender Committee

The Commission managed to hold gender mainstreaming training on June 28, 2024 for the
Gender Committee with facilitators from PSC Academy. The Gender Committee had three
meetings in 2024.

1.2    Contract Management

Finding

The Commission entered into contract for the procurement of seven (7) Toyota Hilux GD 6 and
two (2) Fortuner for a total price of ZWL$205.5 million. The agreed delivery period was eight
(8) weeks. At the time of audit, six (6) motor vehicles were not yet delivered.

Risk/Implication

Financial loss as the vehicles might not be supplied or vehicles of different specifications might
be delivered.

Recommendation

Management should make follow ups with supplier in order to receive outstanding vehicles.

Management Response

The outstanding vehicles are yet to be delivered by the supplier (Earlgrey). The supplier
has already submitted the Bills of Entry of the outstanding vehicles which are awaiting
duty payment. The delay in the delivery was due to flooding of a Toyota vehicle plant in
South Africa, where the supplier had intended to procure from. This then forced the
supplier to look somewhere else for the vehicles. The supplier also indicated that, they
received foreign currency allocation in small batches and it took time to fund one
vehicle as the company had other customers whom they were supposed to supply the
same vehicles.

1.3    Risk Management and Internal Controls

Findings

The Commission did not maintain a robust internal control systems to assist in providing
direction, prevent losses and ensure effective performance. For instance, the Commission lost
77 335 litres worth ZWL$575.5 million of fuel due to fraud committed by the Commission’s
employee. This was contrary to Section 44 (1)(a) (i) of the Public Finance Management Act
[Chapter 22:19] which requires Accounting Officers to maintain effective, efficient and
transparent systems of financial and risk management and internal controls.

In addition, a fraud of ZWL$51.4 million was also perpetrated by staff through manipulation
and falsification of records between the accounting packages.

Risk/ Implication

Financial loss due to misappropriation of financial resources.

Recommendations

Management should implement a robust internal control environment and ensure adherence
thereof.
524

Management should investigate and recover the misappropriated funds.

Management Response

The issue is noted and management has instituted the following changes:

Appointment of the Internal Audit manager to regularly review compliance to laid
internal control systems and best practice. Separated collection, receiving and custody
of fuel within the Administration unit. Introduced the use of requisition forms for fuel
and office provisions; Inspection of registers for fuel and other inventory items on a
regular basis to reduce the chances of fuel losses. The security guards are now
inspecting all deliveries and appending their signatures or stamp as evidence. The issue
was also picked by both the Accounts and Internal Audit Section and was reported to
the Commercial Crimes Division and the matter is under investigation.

1.4    Segregation of Duties

Finding

There was no segregation of duties in the receipting and issuance of fuel as at times one officer
could receive and issue fuel due to staffing challenges in the Administration Unit. These
functions are ordinarily supposed to be performed by different officers.

Risk/Implication

Fraud and error may go undetected.

Recommendation

Management should segregate incompatible duties.

Management Response

The issue is noted and management has instituted the following changes to address
the identified issue:

Separated collection, receiving and custody of fuel within the Administration unit;
Introduced the use of requisition forms for fuel and office provisions. Inspection of
registers for fuel and other inventory items on a regular basis was introduced to reduce
the chances of fuel losses. The Security Guards are now inspecting all deliveries and
append their signatures or stamp as evidence

The Commission was and is still seriously understaffed affecting segregation of duties
as there were only two people (Administration Manager and Officer) in the section.
Instead of three administration officers as per the structure, only one was in post hence
the lack of segregation of duties.

i

FOREWORD

1
SUBMISSION OF ANNUAL REPORT

In terms of Section 309 (2) of the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 20) Act 2013
and Section 10 of the Audit Office Act [Chapter 22:18]  I am required, after examining the
public accounts of Zimbabwe submitted to me in terms of Section 35 (6) and (7) of the
Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19] and signing a certificate recording the
results of such examination, to prepare and submit to the Minister of Finance and Economic
Development, not later than June 30 of each year, a report of my examination and audit of
the public accounts of Zimbabwe.

2
MANDATE OF THE AUDITOR-GENERAL

My duties as set out in the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 20) Act 2013 and
amplified in the Audit Office Act [Chapter 22:18] are: -


to audit the accounts, financial systems and financial management of all departments,
institutions and agencies of government, all provincial and metropolitan councils and all
local authorities;

at the request of government, to carry out special audits of the accounts of any statutory
body or government–controlled entity;

to satisfy myself that the receipt and disbursement of public monies have been made in
accordance with proper authority and has been correctly accounted for and that all
reasonable precautions have been taken to safeguard State property; and

to carry out Value for Money audits, which entail the examination into the economy,
efficiency and effectiveness with which those entrusted with financial and material
resources have utilized them in carrying out their mandates.

3
BASIS OF PREPARATION OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

Management of public funds is governed primarily by the Constitution of Zimbabwe and
provisions of the Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19]. Central Government
uses cash accounting basis for Appropriation Accounts and accruals accounting for Fund
Accounts. Treasury has adopted the International Public Sector Accounting Standards
(IPSAS) as its reporting framework for Central Government which should be fully
implemented by 2025 according to the implementation road map. The Public Accountants
and Auditors Board (PAAB) has the responsibility to set such standards, in terms of section
44 (2) of the Public Accountants and Auditors Act [Chapter 27:12].

4
CONDUCT OF THE AUDIT

My statutory audit is discharged by a programme of test checks and examinations which are
applied in accordance with the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions
(ISSAIs). The checks are intended to provide an overall assurance of the general accuracy
of the accounting transactions and not to disclose each and every error.

I conducted audits at Head Offices of Ministries. Due to COVID-19 travel restrictions and
lockdowns I did not manage to visit outstations. Resources permitting coupled with reduction
in COVID-19 cases, I would like to visit outstations as most Ministries and government
departments have decentralized in line with National Development Strategy (NDS1) and the
devolution strategy, where a number of activities are taking place at district and provincial
level.

ii

Audits of some Appropriation Accounts and Funds were still in progress at the time of
concluding this report mainly due to the backlog created by the pandemic which saw my
2020 report being tabled on March 08, 2022 coupled with the capacity issue of limited staff
numbers, transport challenges and inadequate number of computers.


I also carried out Value for Money and Special Audits on the following areas and the reports
were tabled separately:


Management of Medicines and Allied Substances by the Medicines Control Authority of
Zimbabwe (MCAZ)


Management and Protection of Wetlands by the Environmental Management Agency
(EMA)


COVID 19 Pandemic Financial Management and Utilisation of Public Resources in the
Country’s Provinces by Ministries, Departments and Agencies.

5
STAFF LEVELS, MOVEMENTS, TRAINING AND DEVELOPMENT

Despite efforts to fill vacant posts in 2021, resignations continued to increase during the year
resulting in decrease in staff levels. My Office lost qualified and experienced staff due to
uncompetitive conditions of service. Annexure A shows the staff establishment and
movements during 2021.

While the office continued with some training programmes, the number of in-house
programmes undertaken were reduced due to the limitation of face to face interactions. The
Office was not quite prepared and ready to undertake remote training programmes due to
limited capacity in equipment and connectivity challenges.  Training and development
programmes for articled clerks with ICAZ, ACCA and ICPAZ to which the Office is
accredited continued, however at a slow pace as well.

With the assistance of the African Organisation of English speaking Supreme Audit
Institutions (AFROSAI-E), Development and Technical Partners, my Office participated in
some programmes that were conducted mainly online. My staff continued to attend online
Continuous Professional Development (CPDs) in order to keep abreast with new
developments in the audit profession.

6.        CERTIFICATION OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

I certify that I have examined the Appropriation Accounts, Finance and Revenue Statements
and Fund Accounts of Zimbabwe in accordance with the Constitution of Zimbabwe, the Audit
Office Act [Chapter 22:18] and the Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19].

AUDIT OPINION

I conducted my audit in accordance with International Standards of Supreme Audit
Institutions (ISSAIs). My opinion is on whether the financial statements present fairly the state
of financial affairs in the Ministries, Commissions, Departments and respective Funds. I believe
that the audit evidence I have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for my
opinion of the respective financial statements.



iii

Seventy-six financial statements comprising Appropriation Accounts, Finance and Revenue
Statements and Fund Accounts were audited, and of these, twelve (12) had no issues. The
audit opinions for the accounts are shown in the graph below:



Annexure B shows details of the opinions issued. The financial statements are to be
consolidated into one report by the Accountant-General in terms of section 35 (12) of the
Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19].

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS

I wish to acknowledge efforts rendered by all the Accounting Officers, Receivers of
Revenue, cooperating partners and other stakeholders that made it possible for me to
submit my Report.

My special thanks and gratitude goes to my staff who have continuously demonstrated a
high level of dedication, commitment to duty and support in the production of my report.





HARARE                                                                       M. CHIRI,
June 24, 2022.


                           AUDITOR-GENERAL.







iv


EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


This report covers financial statements which comprise of Appropriation Accounts, Finance and
Revenue Statements and Fund Accounts, highlighting the key audit findings and
recommendations. The objectives of my audit are to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatements, whether
due to fraud or error, to issue an auditor’s report that includes my opinion. I also gave
recommendations on the ways by which issues raised can be addressed with the aim of
improving public sector transparency, accountability and service delivery.
The audit covered financial, compliance and public service delivery aspects on governance
issues, revenue collection and debt management, compensation of employees, procurement of
goods and services, management of assets, and on gender policies and supporting structures.
Guided by the Government thrust on service delivery as enunciated in the National
Development Strategy (NDS 1), my audit also included evaluation of the implementation of
planned programmes by the various entities to ensure achievement of the national strategies
and national vision. An assessment of the progress made in addressing prior year audit
findings was carried out and reported upon.  Those charged with governance in the various
institutions are urged to pay attention to matters raised, so as to improve public sector
transparency, accountability and service delivery.
Below is a graphical overview of the key areas covered during the audit:

v

Key issues raised in this report were mainly on ineffective budget utilisation and control,
unreconciled variances between complementary accounting records, ineffective management
of public resources, payments made from exchequer accounts, ineffective debt recovery
systems, absence of supporting documents, non-delivery of procured assets, inadequate
accounting records and implementation of programmes.
1.
Budget Utilisation and Control
The total allocated budget for Voted funds in terms of the Appropriation (2021) Act, 2020 for 15
Ministries and Commissions included in this report was $91 697 499 187. The Ministries and
Commissions utilised $78 865 410 715 resulting in a total underspending of $12 832 088 472.
The underutilisation of the budget was mainly as a result of non-release of funds by Treasury
due to low revenue inflows. Consequently, this affected achievement of some programme
targets and service delivery by the affected Ministries and Commissions.

2.
Variances between Complementary Accounting Records

There were a number of entities with variances between figures in the financial
statements/returns and corresponding /related accounting records. In some cases, monthly
reconciliations were not being done while in other cases there was no evidence that efforts
were being made to clear the variances noted. This resulted in errors remaining undetected
and not cleared thereby making it difficult to validate the correctness of figures reported.

3.
Management of Public Resources

There were instances where investments were made without the authority of Treasury and
the investments were not disclosed as public financial assets. There is need for Government
through line Ministries to have accurate and up to date records of all investments made so
that Treasury comes up with a consolidated return that is accurate. This will facilitate
following up by line Ministries on receipt of dividends where shares have been acquired and
repayment of loans hence improving on revenue generation.
A total amount of $7 731 437 taken from Funds was used by some Ministries to finance their
Appropriation activities without obtaining Treasury authority. This deprived the Funds from
vi

undertaking planned activities. There was no evidence produced to show that the Funds had
been reimbursed.

4.
Payments made from Exchequer Accounts

The Exchequer Account, an account for receiving revenue was used to make payments
totaling $6 099 800 744 to various service providers during the financial year ended
December 31, 2019.

Furthermore, payments of US$26 714 103, EUR 100 809 and ZAR 385 358 060 were made
from Sub-Exchequer Accounts, which are also revenue receiving accounts. The respective
supporting documents for the payments were not availed. In terms of government
accounting all expenditure is supposed to be paid from the Paymaster General’s Account.
Monies paid from the Exchequer Account may not be properly accounted for and disclosed.

5.
Debt Recovery Systems

There was an increase in non-collection of monies due to Government by the Fund
Accounts. The Fund managers did not apply effective strategies to collect amounts due to
Fund Accounts. Amounts that remained uncollected are indicated in the graph below.
Service delivery remained constrained in the respective Funds as resources were tied in
debtors. If the trend continues the outstanding amounts will be rendered valueless due to
the inflationary environment.



6.
Supporting Documents

Some Ministries did not avail for audit inspection documents relating to payments amounting
to $84 688 794 made to various suppliers of goods and services. Regulations require
transactions to be accurate, complete and supported with adequate documentation.
Therefore, audit could not ascertain the validity of these payments. Unavailability of
supporting documents leads to lack of transparency in the usage of public resources.

  7.
Procurement- Delivery of Assets


An amount of $320 364 074 was paid for procurement of assets by some ministries. Full
payment was made in advance as a precondition of the contracts. However, at the time of
concluding the audit, the suppliers had not delivered the assets. Payments in advance may
result in loss of public funds in the event that the supplier fails to deliver. Public service
delivery is compromised if assets procured are not delivered on time. Annexure D has
details.
vii



Furthermore, there were cases where Ministries were refunded by suppliers who had failed
to deliver. However, the refunds could not procure the same quantities due to inflation.
Ministries should consider including clauses in contracts which will compel service providers
to reimburse funds which will enable them to procure same quantities in the event of a
breach of contract. There is also need for Ministry of Finance and Economic Development in
conjunction with PRAZ to assist MDAs in drafting contract agreements that will safeguard
public resources.

  8.
Accounting Records

Some Departments and Funds did not record some assets in the PFMS, contrary to
Treasury Instructions which require that all assets received from whatever source should be
recorded promptly and accurately in the appropriate manual registers and recorded
immediately on the PFMS. Assets may be misappropriated or converted to personal use if
they are not recorded promptly or if accounting procedures for assets are not followed.

9.
Implementation of Programmes

An evaluation of programme implementation revealed an improvement on the achievement
of set targets. This was attributed to the adoption of programme based budgeting coupled
with monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. Implementation of some of the programs was
curtailed by the Covid-19 pandemic which had a significant negative effect.

However, there is still need to improve on documentation of performance information, as
some entities could not avail non-financial information which indicates planned and achieved
outputs and outcomes and record of budget committee meetings for the 2021 financial year
as required by Treasury circular number 06 of 2019. Consequently, audit was not able to
assess performance of these entities during the financial year under review.

10
PROGRESS IN ADDRESSING PRIOR YEAR AUDIT FINDINGS

The efforts of the Ministries which have taken steps to address the audit findings highlighted
in the 2020 Annual Audit Report of the Auditor-General, are appreciated. Out of 150 audit
findings that were raised, 58 (39%) were fully addressed, 18 (12%) were partly addressed
and 74 (49%) were not addressed. Accounting Officers are urged to fully address the
outstanding audit findings. The progress made is graphically shown below:

Basis for Qualified Opinion

(i)
Sub- Paymaster General’s Account

Finding

The expenditure disclosed in the Appropriation Account of $5 877 874 263 differed with the
Sub-Paymaster General Account balance of $4 835 866 711. From the difference of $1 042
007 552, $985 714 446 was identified as unpresented payments and direct payment made
by Treasury, thus leaving an unreconciled variance of $56 293 106. Under normal
circumstances the two figures are supposed to reconcile. As a result, I could not ascertain
the accuracy and completeness of the figure disclosed in the Appropriation Account.

Risks/Implications

In the absence of a reconciliation of the two figures, the reported financial statements might
have been misstated.

The financial information could be misleading to users and decision makers.


2

Recommendation
